# LinStabPy

> Sparse linear stability and resolvent analysis of compressible viscous flows. Python toolkit (CLI + library) that builds the linearized compressible Navier-Stokes operator on 2D structured base flows and solves eigenvalue and resolvent problems through PETSc/SLEPc with MUMPS sparse-direct factorization.

LinStabPy answers two questions about a steady flow field you supply: stability (does a small disturbance grow on its own, at what frequency, with what shape?) and resolvent (at a given frequency, which harmonic forcing produces the largest response?). Base flows are loaded from files, never computed here. Cases are defined in YAML; results land in contract-stable `.npz` archives.

How to use this file: find the task below, follow the link, and read that page. Links point at human-readable HTML pages; each page's Markdown source lives in the repo under `docs/pages/`.

Critical facts agents get wrong: the `linstabpy` CLI takes NO case arguments -- config and output travel by `LINSTABPY_CASE_CONFIG` and `LINSTABPY_CASE_OUTPUT_NPZ` env vars, and unknown CLI bare words and `--flags` warn on stderr but are otherwise ignored (`parse_known_args`, exit code unchanged), so a guessed command still runs the wrong case. Install is the hard part (one MPI stack, complex-scalar PETSc/SLEPc + MUMPS via `install.sh --diagnose` -> `install.sh` -> `install.sh --check`); nothing that solves will work until `--check` passes. On macOS always use `.venv/bin/python`, never `uv run`. Fixed conventions repo-wide: temporal eigenvalues `omega = eig(i*L0)` with `exp(-i*omega*t)` time dependence, unstable exactly when `Im(omega) > 0`; SBP orders are 2, 4, 6, 8 only; default shifted solve is `KSPPREONLY` + `PCLU` through MUMPS.

## Getting started

Source: https://linstabpy.vercel.app/getting-started/

# Getting started

From a fresh machine to your first spectrum and your first [gain](../core-concepts.md): install the stack, run the examples in the right order, read the outputs, then start your own case. Assumes linear algebra, [MPI](https://grokipedia.com/page/Message_Passing_Interface), and a Unix shell; no prior experience with this codebase needed.

Time budget: install takes 30 to 90 minutes ([PETSc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PETSc) and [SLEPc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SLEPc) compile from source). Example 0 runs in under a minute. The [Blasius](https://grokipedia.com/page/Blasius_boundary_layer) example takes a few minutes on a workstation.

The order that works:

:material-numeric-1-circle: Install with `install.sh` (or conda if you already live there).
:material-numeric-2-circle: Run example 0. It needs no external data and proves the numerics import chain.
:material-numeric-3-circle: Fetch the LinStab2D reference data, run example 1, read its plots.
:material-numeric-4-circle: Run the rest of the family through the runner script.
:material-numeric-5-circle: Write your own YAML case and run it through the driver or a module.

Math conventions used on this page: temporal [eigenvalues](https://grokipedia.com/page/Eigenvalues_and_eigenvectors) are $\omega = \mathrm{eig}(i L_0)$ with $\exp(-i\omega t)$ time dependence, so $\mathrm{Im}(\omega) > 0$ means growth. The [resolvent](https://grokipedia.com/page/Resolvent_formalism) is $H = C F ((\gamma - i\omega) I - L_0)^{-1} F B$. You need these two lines to read any spectrum or gain plot below.


## What you need before you start

**Operating system.** Linux is the reference path. macOS works with one [BLAS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BLAS) caveat (see [macOS and clusters in brief](#macos-and-clusters-in-brief)). Windows is not supported. The installer expects a POSIX shell with `bash`.

**Compilers and tools.** C, C++, and Fortran compilers, plus `make`, `cmake`, `curl`, and `pkg-config`. One MPI stack with development headers (`mpicc`, `mpicxx`, `mpifort`, `mpiexec`). Optional: HDF5 development files, only if you want the MATLAB v7.3 parity tooling.

**The one rule that saves hours.** One MPI stack per install. PETSc, SLEPc, `mpi4py`, `petsc4py`, `slepc4py`, and the `mpiexec` you run with must all come from the same MPI family. Mixing Open MPI headers with an MPICH launcher is the most common broken install. `install.sh --diagnose` exists to catch exactly this before anything compiles.

**Disk and time.** The build directory (`.venv`) holds a full PETSc and SLEPc. Expect several GB and a long compile on first install. Later installs reuse the pattern and go faster.


## Install path A: the reference script

`install.sh` is the supported workstation build: default Python 3.13, PETSc 3.24 with [MUMPS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MUMPS_(software)), complex scalars, editable install of this repo into `.venv`. Run four commands in this order.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/openfluids/linstabpy.git
cd linstabpy

bash install.sh --diagnose
bash install.sh
bash install.sh --check
bash examples/benchmark.sh
```

What each step proves:

| Step | What it does | Success looks like |
|---|---|---|
| `--diagnose` | Read-only host preflight. Checks compilers, MPI launchers, headers, dual-MPI conflicts, and that `mpiexec -n 1 /bin/true` works. Installs nothing. | :white_check_mark: No errors. If it complains, fix the host first. |
| `install.sh` | Creates `.venv`, builds or installs Python with PETSc and SLEPc, repairs `mpi4py` when the wheel ABI mismatches your MPI, installs this repo editable. | :white_check_mark: Ends without error. It never calls `sudo` unless you opt in (see knobs below). |
| `--check` | Verifies `petsc4py` and `slepc4py` import, PETSc uses complex scalars, and a tiny SLEPc non-Hermitian Krylov-Schur solve works from Python. | :white_check_mark: All probes pass. A real-scalar PETSc or a failed NHEP probe means the env is unusable for this code. |
| `examples/benchmark.sh` | Runs a small benchmark (example 0 plus a small example 1) and writes artifacts under `benchmark_runs/<run-id>/`. | :white_check_mark: A fresh run directory with a summary CSV and logs. |

Useful variants:

```bash
bash install.sh --force            # wipe .venv and rebuild everything
bash install.sh --force --latest   # same, but newest compatible releases instead of pins
```

!!! warning "Read the log, do not guess"
    A healthy install prints which MPI launcher configured PETSc and SLEPc, which launcher verified them, the resolved MPI library directory, and single-rank and multi-rank check results. If those paths point at different MPI families, wipe and rebuild from a clean environment. Do not paper over a mixed MPI install with `LD_LIBRARY_PATH`.

Knobs you may need (all in the README with full detail):

| Variable | When to set it |
|---|---|
| `LINSTABPY_AUTO_INSTALL_SYS_DEPS=1` | Let the script call your package manager for missing Linux system tools. |
| `LINSTABPY_SKIP_SYS_DEPS=1` | Skip system dependency checks on provisioned cluster nodes. |
| `LINSTABPY_MPI_STACK=intelmpi` | You already loaded Intel MPI and want it used. |
| `LINSTABPY_PETSC_MPIEXEC=/path/to/mpiexec` | PETSc configure hangs or picks the wrong launcher. |
| `LINSTABPY_VERIFY_MPIEXEC=/path/to/mpiexec` | Install-time checks need a different launcher than configure. |
| `LINSTABPY_MPI4PY_NO_BINARY=1` | Force `mpi4py` to build from source against your active MPI. |
| `LINSTABPY_WITH_H5PY=1` | Also install `h5py` for MATLAB v7.3 file tooling. |

Three launcher knobs, three jobs: `LINSTABPY_PETSC_MPIEXEC` picks the launcher PETSc/SLEPc configure probes, `LINSTABPY_VERIFY_MPIEXEC` picks the launcher install-time checks run under, and `LINSTABPY_MPIEXEC` picks the launcher `examples/run_all_examples.sh` uses. Each defaults to the auto-detected working launcher; set them only when the probe picks the wrong MPI family. `examples/benchmark.sh` re-exports its resolved launcher as `LINSTABPY_MPIEXEC` (and its interpreter as `LINSTABPY_PYTHON_BIN`) for its child runs.

Run everything through `.venv/bin/python` directly (scripts should do this so logs show the interpreter). For interactive shells, `source .venv/bin/activate` is convenient.


## Install path B: conda

Pick conda if you already manage environments that way and want to skip the PETSc compile. conda-forge supplies Python with a complex-scalar PETSc, SLEPc, and `mpi4py` stack. pip then installs only this package, editable, with `--no-deps` so it never pulls a second NumPy or compiles PETSc.

```bash
# Unset these first. A leftover PETSc prefix binds petsc4py to the wrong build.
unset PETSC_DIR PETSC_ARCH SLEPC_DIR

conda env create -f environment.yml
conda activate linstabpy
python -c "import numpy as np; from petsc4py import PETSc; assert np.issubdtype(PETSc.ScalarType, np.complexfloating)"
```

That assert is the whole gate. If it fails, the environment cannot run this code even though `import linstabpy` still works (plain import never touches PETSc by design).

Constraints to know:

* Python is `>=3.11,<3.15` here. conda-forge resolves Python 3.14 with complex PETSc 3.24.
* Never add `petsc4py`, `slepc4py`, or `mpi4py` to the pip list. Those sdists compile PETSc from source and fight the conda MPI stack.
* `environment.yml` is not a second reference build. If conda-forge PETSc differs in minor version from the `install.sh` build, record both versions with your results.
* There is no `environment-gpu.yml`, deliberately. GPU PETSc is not a supported conda path. See [What is still missing](#what-is-still-missing) for the current GPU status.


## The CLI as it really is

This section corrects a mistake that lived in older docs. The `linstabpy` command takes **no case arguments**. It reads everything from environment variables and caches results by config hash. From `src/linstabpy/driver/cli.py`, the only flag is `--version`.

```bash
linstabpy --version        # light: prints version, never initializes PETSc or MPI
linstabpy                  # full run; config and output come from env (below)
python -m linstabpy.driver.cli   # same entrypoint as a module
```

| Variable | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `LINSTABPY_CASE_CONFIG` | none (required) | YAML case file. The CLI stops when it is unset. |
| `LINSTABPY_CASE_OUTPUT_NPZ` | `{prefix}_{config_md5}_{git_sha8}.npz` in cwd | Where the result archive lands. Set a unique path per concurrent run. |
| `LINSTABPY_CASE_LOG_PREFIX` | `linstabpy` | Prefix for log lines and the default output stem. |
| `LINSTABPY_FORCE_RECOMPUTE` | unset | Set to `1`, `true`, `yes`, or `on` (case-insensitive) to skip the cache check and recompute. CLI gate only; library `driver.run` callers always compute. |
| `LINSTABPY_STAGE_HEARTBEAT_SECONDS` | `30` | Progress heartbeat interval for long stages. |

A typical MPI run:

```bash
export LINSTABPY_CASE_CONFIG=cases/my_case.yaml
export LINSTABPY_CASE_OUTPUT_NPZ=results/my_case.npz
mpirun -n 4 linstabpy
```

!!! warning "Unknown arguments warn, then are ignored"
    The CLI uses `parse_known_args`, so `linstabpy run case.yaml` does not error. It prints a warning on stderr (rank 0 only) — for bare words and `--style` options alike — then runs with the env config and drops your words on the floor. If a run used the wrong case, this is the first thing to check. Single-dash PETSc options (plus one following value, e.g. `-ksp_rtol 1e-8`) still pass through to the solver stack.

Caching behavior: on rank 0 the driver loads the existing output NPZ if present and compares its stored config hash and git SHA against the current ones. Match means it prints `Cache valid` and skips the compute. Mismatch or unreadable file means it recomputes. In parameter sweeps, either point each run at its own output path or export `LINSTABPY_FORCE_RECOMPUTE=1` deliberately.

Most examples in `examples/` do **not** go through this CLI. They run as Python modules with their own YAML files (next sections). The driver CLI is for packed-field cases and campaign use.


## macOS and clusters in brief

**macOS.** Same four commands as Linux. One extra step first when possible:

```bash
brew install openblas scalapack
```

Reason: PETSc-downloaded ScaLAPACK can resolve [LAPACK](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LAPACK) symbols to Apple Accelerate inside a Python process, which aborts Python `slepc4py` NHEP solves inside Accelerate `ZLADIV`. The installer prefers Homebrew OpenBLAS and ScaLAPACK at configure time and wraps `.venv/bin/python` so the right BLAS loads first. `install.sh --check` runs a tiny NHEP probe that catches this before examples run. On macOS, always use `.venv/bin/python` directly, never `uv run`, which can bypass the patched layout.

**Clusters.** Load compiler and MPI modules first so the scripts see the same `mpicc`, `mpicxx`, `mpifort`, and `mpiexec` you will run with:

```bash
module load <compiler-module> <mpi-module>
bash install.sh --diagnose
bash install.sh
bash install.sh --check
```

For Intel MPI with oneAPI, source `setvars.sh`, export `LINSTABPY_MPI_STACK=intelmpi` plus the `I_MPI_CC/CXX/F90/FC` compiler variables, then run the same sequence. Full commands live in the README install section.

**Thread policy for every MPI run.** One thread per rank unless you are benchmarking deliberately:

```bash
export OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 MKL_NUM_THREADS=1 OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1
export NUMEXPR_NUM_THREADS=1 VECLIB_MAXIMUM_THREADS=1
```

Without this, each rank spawns a full BLAS thread pool and [sparse](https://grokipedia.com/page/Sparse_matrix) direct solves get slower, not faster. More ranks are not automatically faster for factorization either. Compare rank counts on your machine.


## First run: example 0, no data needed

Example 0 validates curvilinear derivatives. It is pure NumPy, runs single-process, and needs no reference files. Run it first. If it fails, the problem is your Python environment, not MPI or data.

```bash
.venv/bin/python -m examples.linstab2d.example_0_curvilinear_validation
```

Outputs, next to the script: `example_0_curvilinear_validation.npz` (numbers), `.log` (run log), and PNGs including the curvilinear mesh figure and a field-derivative triptych. Open the triptych. It shows the test field and its discrete derivatives on the deformed mesh. This is also your first look at the [SBP](https://grokipedia.com/page/Summation_by_parts) operators in action: the derivatives stay clean at boundaries, which is the whole point of the validated closures.

Re-plot any time without recomputing:

```bash
.venv/bin/python -m examples.linstab2d.example_0_plots
```


## Second run: Blasius resolvent

Example 1 is the real first science run: resolvent gains with optimal forcing and [response modes](../core-concepts.md) for a [compressible](https://grokipedia.com/page/Compressible_flow) Blasius [boundary layer](https://grokipedia.com/page/Boundary_layer) ($Re = 6.0\times 10^5$, $Ma = 0.3$, SBP order 4, grid $300 \times 100$). It needs the MATLAB base flow `BL_BF.mat`. The repo ships it in `examples/linstab2d/baseflows/`, and the loader reads it from there, so a fresh clone runs the example.

To read the base flows from a LinStab2D clone instead, fetch the reference data once:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/LinStab2D/LinStab2D.git ~/linstab2d-reference
export LINSTABPY_BASEFLOW_DATA_DIR=$HOME/linstab2d-reference
```

The variable is optional. The example raises `FileNotFoundError` only when the file is missing from the configured directory (the default one or the one the variable names). The Song and Savarino cases ship their own data or fetch scripts and never read this variable.

Run the case, then the plots:

```bash
.venv/bin/python -m examples.linstab2d.example_1_blasius
.venv/bin/python -m examples.linstab2d.example_1_plots
```

What you get:

* `example_1_blasius.npz`: gains, forcing and response modes, mesh, [Chu](../core-concepts.md) weights, BC provenance, solver metadata. Load with `numpy.load`. The key names form a compatibility surface documented in the [runtime NPZ contract](../development/runtime-npz-contract.md).
* `example_1_blasius_baseflow.png`: the mean flow you linearized about. Always look at this before trusting modes.
* `example_1_blasius_modes_forcing_response_{u,v}[_imag]_mosaic.png`: one mosaic per component. Each shows the optimal forcing (what to inject), the response (what grows), and their imaginary parts.

How to read the mosaic: the forcing panel is the input shape $v$, the response panel is $u = Hv/\sigma$, and the gain $\sigma$ printed on the figure is their energy ratio in the Chu norm. A large gain with a clean, smooth mode pair is the expected picture. Noise or grid-scale wiggles point at resolution, filter, or boundary setup, not at the solver.

![Blasius base flow: streamwise velocity with the boundary layer developing downstream](figures/example_1_blasius_baseflow.png)

*The mean flow you linearize about. Always look at this before trusting modes.*

![Blasius optimal forcing (left) and response (right) for the streamwise velocity component](figures/example_1_blasius_modes_forcing_response_u_mosaic.png)

*What a healthy answer looks like: smooth, cleanly separated forcing and response structures. Compare your run against this before tuning anything.*

The case definition lives in `examples/linstab2d/example_1_blasius.yaml`: physics, grid, sponge, frequency, mode count, BC recipe, solver policy, each with a comment. YAML keeps the explanation next to the knob, which is why the repo uses it instead of long flag lists. [Your first own case](#your-first-own-case) walks a trimmed version.


## The example family map

Six Martini examples form the core family. Run one, run all, then compare against MATLAB:

```bash
bash examples/run_all_examples.sh --list        # what exists
bash examples/run_all_examples.sh --example 1 --skip-parity   # one example, no MATLAB check
bash examples/run_all_examples.sh               # everything plus parity and plots
```

| # | Module | What it teaches | Needs |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | `example_0_curvilinear_validation` | SBP derivatives on deformed meshes | Nothing. Pure NumPy. |
| 1 | `example_1_blasius` | Resolvent gains, forcing and response | `BL_BF.mat` (bundled) |
| 2 | `example_2_jet` | Resolvent on a turbulent jet base flow | `M09jet.mat` (bundled) |
| 3 | `example_3_streaky_bl` | Temporal and spatial EVP plus Floquet options | MATLAB fixtures for plots |
| 4 | `example_4_cavity` | Direct and adjoint eigenvalues, spectra | `Step_BF.mat` via data dir |
| 5 | `example_5_paraboloid` | Resolvent on a 3D body-fitted mesh | `Paraboloid_BF.mat` via data dir |

Each example has a matching `example_N_plots.py` that renders figures from the NPZ without recomputing. The runner calls compute then plots automatically. Direct module invocation writes the NPZ only.

MPI form, with PETSc options passed after `--`:

```bash
bash examples/run_all_examples.sh --mpi -n 10 -m examples.linstab2d.example_3_streaky_bl
bash examples/run_all_examples.sh --mpi -n 1 -m examples.linstab2d.example_1_blasius -- -eps_monitor
```

Without `-n`, the runner defaults to half the detected physical cores. Override the launcher with `LINSTABPY_MPIEXEC` and the rank count with `LINSTABPY_MPI_RANKS` when the machine needs explicit paths. Interpreter: `LINSTABPY_PYTHON` wins over `LINSTABPY_PYTHON_BIN`, else `.venv/bin/python`.

Beyond Martini, three case families cover harder ground. Leave them for week two:

| Family | What it is | Data story | How to run |
|---|---|---|---|
| `examples/song/` | Song and Robinet SWBLI global stability, $\theta = 32°$ | Ships packed `song_32deg.npz` for checks; full pipeline needs Plot3D `grid.grd` + `mean_flow.dat` in `inputs/raw/` | `prepare_baseflow`, `plot_baseflow`, then `mpiexec -n 4 python -m examples.song.song --config ...` |
| `examples/sawtooth/` | Lui 2022 suction-side SWBLI, stride-2 field | Ships packed `sawtooth.npz` ($300 \times 340$) | Baseflow figure, `mpiexec -n 4` EVP run, spectrum figure. See its README. |
| `examples/savarino/` | 30.8° SWBLI resolvent gain maps and backend benchmarks | `fetch_zenodo.py` downloads the Tecplot base flow | Slurm campaign scripts. Validation and speed reproduction, not new physics. |

Parity checks compare Python results against MATLAB reference exports:

```bash
.venv/bin/python examples/linstab2d/compare_martini_examples.py
```

Missing reference bundles skip cleanly here (silent in CI) and validate when present locally. The pytest parity marker behaves more strictly; see [Verify with tests and benchmarks](#verify-with-tests-and-benchmarks).


### What things cost

No maintained per-example runtime table exists yet, but two measured anchors calibrate expectations. Both come from the Savarino case on one c9 node (dual Xeon Silver 4210R, 20 cores, MKL), August 2026, recorded in `examples/savarino/*.csv` with commit, ranks, and Slurm job per row.

Single resolvent point, Mack point, 450,000 unknowns, 23.4M nonzeros, MUMPS (strong scaling, jobs run serially):

| Ranks | Wall (s) | Peak RSS (GiB) | Gain |
|---|---|---|---|
| 4 | 190.5 | 18.6 | 179.1173862845 |
| 8 | 154.6 | 25.4 | 179.1173862854 |
| 16 | 148.2 | 40.6 | 179.1173862846 |

Read it as: gains identical to 10 digits, ranks 4 to 16 buy 22 percent less time for twice the memory. Factorization dominates; more ranks are not automatically faster.

Full 200-point gain map, same hardware, 5 jobs concurrent on 20 cores: 83.6 minutes as independent per-point jobs, 59.7 minutes through the line driver with anchor reuse. The router earns its keep on dense grids.

Measure your own runs the same way: `examples/benchmark.sh` writes wall times and logs under `benchmark_runs/<run-id>/`, and every result NPZ carries `cost_wall_*` keys plus provenance. When reporting a slow machine, send those plus the `--diagnose` output.

## The tutorial PDF

`docs/tutorial/tutorial.pdf` walks the Martini examples figure by figure. Section 5 explains how to read the baseflow, spectrum, and mosaic figures. The PDF is not tracked in git, so build it:

```bash
cd docs/tutorial && make tutorial.pdf   # needs pdflatex
```

`make clean` removes build artifacts. If you lack a TeX distribution, the example PNGs plus [Second run: Blasius resolvent](#second-run-blasius-resolvent) cover the same ground without the prose.


## Your first own case

You have two ways to run custom work. Example modules for MATLAB-parity style studies with generated meshes. Packed-field cases through the driver for your own base flows. This section sketches the packed-field route, which is the one new research takes.

**A case is a YAML file plus baseflow arrays.** The YAML names physics, grid, sponge, boundary recipe, analysis targets, and solver policy. The baseflow is eight arrays with fixed names: `x`, `y`, `rho`, `u`, `v`, `w`, `T`, `sponge`. The loader reads either an `npz` archive or a directory of `npy` files. It never guesses filenames; the YAML names the file.

Trimmed from the Blasius YAML, the shape of every case:

```yaml
Re: 6.0e5        # Reynolds number, rho_ref U_ref L_ref / mu(T_0)
Ma: 0.3          # Mach number, U_ref / sqrt(kappa R T_ref)
Pr: 0.7          # Prandtl number
kappa: 1.4       # heat capacity ratio (gamma in most textbooks)
T_0: 273.15      # freestream static temperature [K]

nx: 300
ny: 100
fd_order: 4      # SBP interior order: 2, 4, 6, or 8

sponge:
  amplitude: 5.0
  xs_trans: 0.02
  # ... ramp widths and offsets that keep outgoing waves from reflecting

bc:
  penalty: 1.0e4
  recipe:
    - {type: dirichlet, borders: lrbt, variables: uvwT}

solver:
  # eigen targets, tolerances, backend selection
```

Three details that bite newcomers:

1. **Nondimensionalization is convective.** Density, velocity, and temperature equal 1 in the freestream. Pressure never appears explicitly; the nondimensional [ideal gas law](https://grokipedia.com/page/Ideal_gas_law) is $p^* = \rho^* T^* / (\kappa Ma^2)$. If your base flow comes from an acoustically scaled LES code, convert first. The README nondimensionalization section has the exact factors.
2. **Boundary recipes are data.** Each rule names a type (`dirichlet` or `neumann`), border letters (`l`, `r`, `t`, `b`, combined like `lt`), and variable blocks (`u`, `T`, `ruvw`, `ruvwT`). [Neumann](https://grokipedia.com/page/Neumann_boundary_condition) rules usually want `exclude_corners: true` and, on deformed meshes, `curvilinear_normals: true`. Assembly applies BC rows last and publishes the free degree sets downstream solvers must use. The `penalty` beside the recipe pins Dirichlet DOFs (diagonal value after row and column zeroing) and scales Neumann rows; keep the default unless leakage diagnostics complain. Full mechanics in [core concepts](../core-concepts.md).
3. **The dissipation epsilon has two halves.** Building the dissipation operator and setting its strength are separate flags, and setting only one is a silent no-op. The Workflow page documents the exact pair. On rectilinear meshes you usually want it off; on meshes curved in both directions you usually want it on.

Run the case through the driver ([The CLI as it really is](#the-cli-as-it-really-is) for the env vars), then inspect the archive:

```python
import numpy as np

d = np.load("results/my_case.npz")
print(d["omega"])  # temporal eigenvalues near your target
print(d["gains"])  # resolvent gains, if a resolvent stage ran
print(d["provenance_config_hash"], d["provenance_linstabpy_git_sha"])
```

Keep the YAML next to the NPZ. That pair, plus the git SHA inside the archive, is what makes the run reproducible and is what the stability acceptance postchecks (see the [runtime NPZ contract](../development/runtime-npz-contract.md)) validate against.

Before trusting any spectrum, check the basics the README lists in full: requested `nev` versus converged `nconv`, subspace size `ncv`, [EPS](../solver-glossary.md) tolerance and convergence test, postcheck residuals, boundary leakage, and target distances. Converged Ritz pairs with bad full-operator residuals happen on interior non-Hermitian problems, and the postcheck is what catches them.


## Verify with tests and benchmarks

The test suite has three lanes:

```bash
.venv/bin/python -m pytest --collect-only tests   # what exists
.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/                 # default lane
LINSTABPY_MATLAB_PARITY=1 .venv/bin/python -m pytest -m matlab_parity   # MATLAB comparisons
```

Deliberate semantics: :white_check_mark: parity tests are **deselected** by default, not skipped, so they never pad the skip count. Every skip in a default run names an absent optional backend ([STRUMPACK](https://portal.nersc.gov/project/sparse/strumpack/), [CUDA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CUDA), `superlu_dist`) on your machine. But once you request parity with the env var, a missing reference is a :x: **failure**, not a skip. A requested comparison that silently does nothing is worse than useless.

Tracked files must stay under 60 MiB each:

```bash
.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/test_tracked_file_size.py -q
```

Large generated outputs, raw MATLAB exports, and machine-local benchmark products stay out of git. Regenerate or archive them externally.

`examples/benchmark.sh` artifacts live under `benchmark_runs/<run-id>/` with a summary CSV and logs. Send those plus full `--diagnose` and install output when reporting a broken machine.


## Troubleshooting quick map

| Symptom | Likely cause | First check |
|---|---|---|
| MPI compile failure, `mpi.h` missing | Missing dev headers | Install your MPI stack dev package (for example `libopenmpi-dev`), or load the full cluster module. |
| PETSc built against one MPI, launched with another | Dual-MPI environment | Pick one stack, put it first in `PATH`, wipe `.venv`, reinstall. Never mix. |
| `mpi4py` import fails after switching MPI | Wheel ABI mismatch | Wipe `.venv`, then `LINSTABPY_MPI4PY_NO_BINARY=1 bash install.sh`. |
| Python NHEP solve aborts on macOS, C SLEPc works | Accelerate LAPACK interposition | `brew install openblas scalapack`, reinstall, use `.venv/bin/python` only. |
| PETSc configure hangs | Wrong launcher probed | `LINSTABPY_PETSC_MPIEXEC=/path/to/working/mpiexec bash install.sh`. |
| Example raises `FileNotFoundError` for `.mat` | The `.mat` file is missing from `examples/linstab2d/baseflows/`, or from the directory `LINSTABPY_BASEFLOW_DATA_DIR` names | Restore the file, or point `LINSTABPY_BASEFLOW_DATA_DIR` at a LinStab2D clone (optional override). |
| `linstabpy` ran the wrong case | Args ignored (stderr warning, exit 0) | The CLI takes no case args. Set `LINSTABPY_CASE_CONFIG` and rerun. |
| Stale results reused | Cache hit | Check for the `Cache valid` line. Set unique output paths or `LINSTABPY_FORCE_RECOMPUTE=1`. |
| Factor crash or OOM | Backend, ranks, or memory | Verify backend build, raise ranks, consider BLR options, check BC setup. |

The [Troubleshooting](../troubleshooting.md) page carries the full commands for each row.


## What is still missing

Honest gaps, so you can plan around them:

* **No GPU install path.** `cudss` (through `nvmath-python`, wrapped around [FGMRES](https://grokipedia.com/page/Generalized_minimal_residual_method)) is the validated GPU route and matches MUMPS to 1e-12 on tested cases, but there is no one-command GPU environment. `install.sh --stack gpu-strumpack --dry-run` only prints a plan. CPU with MUMPS stays the default you should build on.
* **No Windows support.** POSIX shell and Unix MPI are assumed throughout.
* **Reference `.mat` files are external.** The four Martini base flows live in a LinStab2D clone you fetch yourself. Nothing in this repo vendors them, for provenance and size reasons.
* **No per-example runtime table yet.** Wall times depend on grid, ranks, and backend. [The example family map](#the-example-family-map) has Savarino reference anchors (single point scaling plus a 200-point map) and the measurement protocol; Martini per-example timings are still unmeasured contributions welcome.
* **Tutorial PDF needs a TeX toolchain.** `pdflatex` must be installed to build it. There is no hosted HTML version of the tutorial.
* **Spatial and map entry points are library-first.** Temporal EVP and single-frequency resolvent have the smoothest CLI story. Spatial solves and $\beta$ and $\omega$ maps are best driven through module entry points and the `resolvent_map` API today.
* **Error messages assume context.** Backend probing fails loudly (good), but some PETSc-level errors still surface raw. Paste them with the benchmark artifacts when asking for help.


## Where to go next

* Run the family: [example family map](#the-example-family-map) commands, then the parity comparison.
* Read [Core concepts](../core-concepts.md) for scope and vocabulary.
* Read the [Architecture](../architecture.md) page before writing your own YAML. It documents stage order, the dissipation pair, and acceptance gates.
* Open one [module guide](../modules/index.md) package note when you need math or code detail. Start with LNSE Operator Assembly or Resolvent Analysis.
* Keep the [Boundaries](../boundaries.md) page open while building cases. It lists every env var, flag, and output key.
* Open the [solver glossary](../solver-glossary.md) beside any solver output.
* Citing results: see [Cite linstabpy](../index.md#cite-linstabpy) and the [references](../references.md) page. The glossary defines `KSP`, `PC`, `EPS`, `ST`, and `MatShell`, with links to the official docs.

If something on this page failed for you, that is a documentation bug worth reporting. Say which section, paste the command and the error, and attach the `--diagnose` output.

## Boundary interfaces

Source: https://linstabpy.vercel.app/boundaries/

# Boundary interfaces

This page is the reference for how you talk to LinStabPy from outside: CLI commands, YAML cases, Python imports, file inputs, and output files. Math conventions match the rest of the docs: $\omega = \mathrm{eig}(i L_0)$, unstable exactly when $\mathrm{Im}(\omega) > 0$, [resolvent](https://grokipedia.com/page/Resolvent_formalism) $H = C F (L_0 - (\gamma + i\omega) I)^{-1} F B$.

## Command line interface

### linstabpy (driver CLI)

**Description**: Command-line entry for the shared case driver. It takes no case arguments. It reads the case path and output path from environment variables, checks the result cache by config hash and git SHA on rank 0, and either reuses cached results or runs the full driver (preflight, operator assembly, [PETSc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PETSc) and [SLEPc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SLEPc) solves, IO, provenance).

**Source file**: `src/linstabpy/driver/cli.py`

**Flags**:

- `--version`: optional. Print the installed package version and exit without initializing PETSc or [MPI](https://grokipedia.com/page/Message_Passing_Interface).

**Environment** (the real CLI surface, generated from `CLI_ENV_VARS`):

<!-- GENERATED:CLI-ENV-START -->
- `LINSTABPY_CASE_CONFIG`: YAML case file. The CLI stops when it is unset. Default `none (required)`.
- `LINSTABPY_CASE_OUTPUT_NPZ`: Result archive path. Default `{prefix}_{config_md5}_{git_sha8}.npz in the working directory`.
- `LINSTABPY_CASE_LOG_PREFIX`: Log-line prefix and default output stem. Default `linstabpy`.
- `LINSTABPY_FORCE_RECOMPUTE`: Set to 1, true, yes, or on to skip the cache check (CLI gate only; library runs always compute). Default `unset (cache check runs)`.
- `LINSTABPY_STAGE_HEARTBEAT_SECONDS`: Progress heartbeat interval in float seconds. Default `30`.
- `LINSTABPY_CASE_ROOT_ASSEMBLY`: Root-only assembly for iterative eigen ST solvers; stability-only. Default `unset (auto: on for iterative eigen ST solvers under MPI)`.
<!-- GENERATED:CLI-ENV-END -->

!!! warning "Unknown arguments warn, then are ignored"
    The parser uses `parse_known_args`, so extra words on the command line do not error. Bare words and `--style` options print a `warning: ignoring unknown arguments [...]` line on stderr (rank 0 only) and the run continues with the env config; the exit code is unchanged. Single-dash PETSc options (`-ksp_monitor`, ...), plus one following value (`-ksp_rtol 1e-8`), still pass through to the solver stack. There is no `run` subcommand and no `--config` flag. An older revision of this page documented both. They never existed. Unknown `LINSTABPY_*` names in the environment get the same treatment: a stderr warning with a did-you-mean hint (registry: `src/linstabpy/config/env_registry.py`), then ignored.

**Usage examples**:

```bash
linstabpy --version
```

```bash
export LINSTABPY_CASE_CONFIG=path/to/case.yaml
export LINSTABPY_CASE_OUTPUT_NPZ=results/out.npz
mpiexec -n 8 linstabpy
```

```bash
python -m linstabpy.driver.cli
```

### YAML case configuration interface

**Description**: External configuration boundary for scientific cases. Users interact primarily by editing YAML case files that define baseflow paths, physics, numerics (including [finite-difference](https://grokipedia.com/page/Finite_difference_method) orders), boundary conditions, eigen/resolvent parameters, and solver policy. Files are ingested with a SafeLoader that accepts scientific floats, then structurally validated (TOP_LEVEL_ALLOWED keys such as paths/physics/numerics and related blocks).

**Source File**: `src/linstabpy/utils/yaml_io.py; src/linstabpy/config/schema.py; src/linstabpy/utils/_solver_cfg.py`

**Arguments**:

- `config path` (str | Path): required - Filesystem path passed to load_config(path) returning a dict for driver/solvers.

**Options**:

- `paths`(mapping): optional - Top-level block for input/output paths (baseflow npy/npz dumps, mesh, artifacts).
- `physics`(mapping): optional - Top-level physics parameters for the linearized [compressible](https://grokipedia.com/page/Compressible_flow) [Navier-Stokes](https://grokipedia.com/page/Navier–Stokes_equations) problem.
- `numerics`(mapping): optional - Top-level numerics block including finite-difference order settings traversed by validation helpers.
- `bc`(mapping): optional - Boundary recipe block: ordered `recipe` rules plus `penalty` (Dirichlet diagonal pin and Neumann row scale; driver default `1e8`, library and router default `1e4`).
- `complex / int list fields`(complex | list[complex] | list[int]): optional - Loosely typed YAML scalars/lists parsed into Python complex and int lists (parse_complex, parse_complex_list, parse_int_list) for frequencies, [wavenumbers](https://grokipedia.com/page/Wavenumber), and similar solver inputs.

<!-- GENERATED:YAML-KEYS-START -->
**Top-level keys** (`TOP_LEVEL_ALLOWED`, generated — 75 keys):

`L_cavity`, `Lx`, `Ly`, `Ma`, `Pr`, `Re`, `St`, `T_0`, `alpha_filter`, `alpha_temp`, `analysis`, `assembly_backend`, `baseflow_input`, `baseflow_preprocess`, `bc`, `bc_mask_layout`, `beta`, `cases`, `coarsen`, `conformal_scale`, `dedupe_tol`, `deform`, `dx`, `fd_order`, `floquet_shift`, `forcing_zero_vars`, `kappa`, `kx`, `logging`, `m`, `mask_x_left`, `mask_x_right`, `matlab_parity_dmudt`, `model`, `n_modes`, `n_modes_resolvent`, `n_modes_stability`, `n_periods`, `ncv`, `numerics`, `nx`, `ny`, `omega`, `omega_shift_fallback`, `omega_target`, `paths`, `penalty`, `physics`, `preprocess`, `run_resolvent`, `run_spatial`, `run_stability`, `run_temporal`, `schema_version`, `solver`, `spatial_omega_imag_shift`, `sponge`, `stability_search_extra_modes`, `stride_eta`, `stride_ksi`, `temporal_quotas`, `temporal_targets`, `use_omega_shift_fallback`, `x_cavity_start`, `x_max_base`, `x_min_factor`, `x_periodicity`, `xrange`, `y_i`, `y_max`, `y_stretch_yi`, `y_symmetry`, `yrange`, `zero_dmudT`, `zero_dmudT_martini_parity`

SBP `fd_order` values allowed: 2, 4, 6, 8.
<!-- GENERATED:YAML-KEYS-END -->

**Usage Examples**:

```bash
load_config('cases/blasius_resolvent.yaml')
```

```bash
# case.yaml top-level keys constrained by validate_config / TOP_LEVEL_ALLOWED
```

### make (tutorial docs build)

**Description**: Secondary CLI boundary for building the tutorial PDF documentation with pdflatex (not part of the solver runtime).

**Source File**: `docs/tutorial/Makefile`

**Usage Examples**:

```bash
make all
```

```bash
make clean
```

```bash
make tutorial.pdf
```

## Integration Suggestions

### Python library import (lazy public API)

Embed LinStabPy in larger openfluids or research pipelines by importing the package. Public symbols resolve on first attribute access so a plain import stays lightweight and does not eagerly initialize PETSc/MPI. Suitable for stability, [adjoint](https://grokipedia.com/page/Adjoint), [structural sensitivity](core-concepts.md), and resolvent workflows after the caller supplies baseflow data and config.

**Example Code**:

```
import linstabpy
# Heavy solvers load only on first attribute access
print(linstabpy.__version__)  # version without PETSc init
# Configure via YAML dict or SolverConfig, then call driver/stability/resolvent APIs
```

<!-- GENERATED:PYTHON-API-START -->
**Public names** (`_LAZY_EXPORTS`, generated — 9 names):

| Public name | Module | Attribute |
|---|---|---|
| `BaseFlow` | `linstabpy.baseflow` | `BaseFlow` |
| `adjoint_eigenvalues` | `linstabpy.stability._eigenvalues` | `adjoint_eigenvalues` |
| `build_lnse_operator` | `linstabpy.operators.assembly` | `build_lnse_operator` |
| `build_lnse_system` | `linstabpy.operators.assembly` | `build_lnse_system` |
| `compute_chu_norm` | `linstabpy.operators.energy_norm` | `compute_chu_norm` |
| `resolvent_analysis` | `linstabpy.resolvent.analysis` | `resolvent_analysis` |
| `resolvent_map` | `linstabpy.solvers.router.resolvent_map` | `resolvent_map` |
| `temporal_eigenvalues` | `linstabpy.stability._eigenvalues` | `eigenvalues` |
| `wavemaker` | `linstabpy.stability.sensitivity` | `wavemaker` |
<!-- GENERATED:PYTHON-API-END -->

**Best Practices**:

- Rely on lazy __getattr__ so import-time side effects stay minimal
- Call PETSc/MPI initialization explicitly only when entering solver paths
- Pass validated config dicts (validate_config) rather than ad-hoc nested structures
- Prefer SolverConfig / from_config so YAML, env, and defaults share one precedence model

### YAML case file + driver orchestration

Standard user-facing integration for batch and HPC runs: prepare mean-flow fields (npy/npz), write a Martini/Song-style YAML case, validate, and run through the driver CLI under MPI. Outputs are stability/resolvent artifacts, metrics, and provenance payloads.

**Example Code**:

```
# case.yaml defines paths, physics, numerics, eigen/resolvent, solver policy
from linstabpy.utils.yaml_io import load_config
from linstabpy.config.schema import validate_config
cfg = load_config('case.yaml')
validate_config(cfg, source='case.yaml')
# Then invoke driver.run / CLI entry with the merged config
```

**Best Practices**:

- Keep dissipation apply flags aligned across stability and resolvent stages
- Use schema validation before long MPI jobs to fail fast on unknown keys
- Store baseflow and mesh paths relative to a reproducible case directory
- Document expected artifacts alongside the case (module + NPZ name); the live example list is `examples/run_all_examples.sh` `EXAMPLE_SPECS`

### PETSc / SLEPc / MUMPS / optional cuDSS backend

External numerical stack integration. Core install uses NumPy/SciPy/PyYAML; extras enable HDF5, parallel PETSc/SLEPc (mpi4py, petsc4py, slepc4py), and optional GPU [cuDSS](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cudss/). [MUMPS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MUMPS_(software)) ordering names are shared via mumps_options without importing PETSc at module load.

**Example Code**:

```
# Install core + parallel stack
# pip install 'linstabpy[petsc]'  # or conda via environment.yml
# Optional: pip install 'linstabpy[hdf5]' 'linstabpy[cudss]'
# Runtime: export LINSTABPY_CASE_CONFIG=case.yaml && mpiexec -n N linstabpy
```

**Best Practices**:

- Install matching mpi4py/petsc4py/slepc4py builds for the cluster MPI
- Select MUMPS ordering (amd/pord/metis/qamd/auto) consistently in config
- Treat cuDSS as optional GPU factor path shelled through PETSc PC
- Do not import PETSc-dependent modules at package import time; follow lazy init patterns

### CFD baseflow data stores (file I/O)

Ingest on-disk mean-flow fields as npy directories or npz archives (density, velocity components, temperature, mesh, sponge) produced by external nonlinear [CFD](https://grokipedia.com/page/Computational_fluid_dynamics). LinStabPy does not generate baseflows; integration starts at load/preprocess boundaries under baseflow/.

**Example Code**:

```
# paths block in case.yaml points at baseflow archives
# paths:
#   baseflow: ./data/meanflow.npz
#   output: ./artifacts/
```

**Best Practices**:

- Provide structured-mesh-compatible fields expected by grid_fields/preprocess
- Apply sponge and shock-cleanup options via config rather than ad-hoc scripts
- Version baseflow dumps alongside YAML for provenance
