## Core concepts

Source: https://linstabpy.vercel.app/core-concepts/

# Core concepts

Short, exact definitions of the physics and math vocabulary used across this wiki. Each entry states what the thing is, the convention this repo uses, and where to read more. Solver objects (`KSP`, `PC`, `EPS`, `ST`, `MatShell`) live in the [solver glossary](solver-glossary.md). Code structure lives in the [module guide](modules/index.md).

Shared conventions: the perturbation state is $q' = [\rho', u', v', w', T']^T$ per grid point; the assembled operator satisfies $\partial_t q' = L_0 q'$ in the interior; temporal eigenvalues are $\omega = \mathrm{eig}(i L_0)$ with $\exp(-i\omega t)$ time dependence.


## Stability vocabulary

**Base flow.** A steady solution $\bar q(x, y)$ of the compressible [Navier-Stokes](https://grokipedia.com/page/Navier–Stokes_equations) equations, loaded from files and never computed here. Starting point of every analysis. Nondimensional, convective scaling: freestream density, velocity, and temperature equal 1. See [base flow](modules/baseflow.md).

**Perturbation.** The small disturbance $q'(x, y, z, t)$ about the base flow. LinStabPy solves linear equations for $q'$ only. Nonlinear saturation is out of scope by construction.

**Discrete temporal operator.** The assembled sparse matrix $iL_0$ whose [eigenvalues](https://grokipedia.com/page/Eigenvalues_and_eigenvectors) are the reported $\omega$. "Discrete" marks it as the matrix acting on grid vectors, as opposed to the continuous linearized operator. Every temporal eigensolve targets this matrix through shift-invert; the $i$ puts frequencies on the real axis and growth rates on the imaginary axis under the $\exp(-i\omega t)$ convention.

**Temporal growth rate.** The imaginary part $\mathrm{Im}(\omega)$ of a temporal [eigenvalue](https://grokipedia.com/page/Eigenvalues_and_eigenvectors). Mode amplitude evolves as $\exp(\mathrm{Im}(\omega)\, t)$, so positive means exponential growth in time at a fixed station. Reported for every accepted mode with its postcheck residual.

**Angular frequency.** The real part $\mathrm{Re}(\omega)$. Oscillations run as $\exp(-i\,\mathrm{Re}(\omega)\, t)$. [Shift-invert](solver-glossary.md) targets in YAML live in full complex $\omega$ space, so you aim at a frequency and growth rate together.

**Direct mode.** A right eigenvector of the stability problem: the spatial shape $v(x, y)$ of the disturbance. Modes are normalized in the Chu norm (or $L^2$ where stated) before any comparison or plot.

**Spatial amplification.** At prescribed real spanwise [wavenumber](https://grokipedia.com/page/Wavenumber) $\beta$ and real frequency $\omega$, the spatial problem returns a complex streamwise wavenumber $\alpha$. Amplification along $x$ is read from $\mathrm{Im}(\alpha)$ while following one branch; the sign interpretation depends on the branch, so never judge convective or absolute behavior from a single point. Build the spectrum first, then track the branch. See the tutorial and [stability analysis](modules/stability.md).

**Generalized eigenvalue problem.** An eigenproblem of the form $A x = \lambda B x$ with $B \neq I$ (see [generalized eigenvectors](https://grokipedia.com/page/Generalized_eigenvector)). Ours is the spatial pencil $(L_c + \omega L_w)\, v = \alpha\, R\, v$. Boundary rows make $R$ singular, so $\lambda = \infty$ eigenvalues exist for the constrained subspace. Tiny or near-full problems go to dense [QZ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/QZ_algorithm), which handles singular $B$ natively; production sizes use shift-invert [EPS](solver-glossary.md).

**Boundary layer.** The thin region near a solid wall where viscosity brings the flow from freestream speed to rest at the wall. Blasius flow, the base flow of example 1, is the flat-plate similarity solution of the [boundary-layer](https://grokipedia.com/page/Boundary_layer) equations. Background: [Scholarpedia: Boundary Layer Theory](http://www.scholarpedia.org/article/Boundary_Layer_Theory).


## Resolvent vocabulary

**Modal vs non-modal.** Modal stability asks about $t \to \infty$: do all eigenvalues sit on the stable side. Non-modal stability asks about finite time: how far can a perturbation wander before (possibly) decaying. For normal operators the answers agree; for non-normal ones they can differ wildly, and the finite-time answer is an optimization problem, not an eigenvalue. See Frantz, Loiseau and Robinet (2023), *Krylov methods for large-scale dynamical systems*, *Appl. Mech. Rev.* 75(3), 030802, modal and non-modal stability.

**Resolvent.** The operator $H = C F ((\gamma - i\omega) I - L_0)^{-1} F B$ mapping harmonic forcing to harmonic response at frequency $\omega$. Mathematically an instance of the [resolvent formalism](https://grokipedia.com/page/Resolvent_formalism). $B$ and $C$ restrict inputs and outputs (regions, variables), $F$ is an optional spatial filter inside the masks, $\gamma \ge 0$ is the discount below. Never formed as entries; applied through one factorization. The resolvent is the frequency-domain analogue of optimal-perturbation analysis below: same question (worst input, largest output), asked per frequency instead of per time horizon. The sign of $\omega$ follows $\exp(-i\omega t)$, as for the eigenvalues; see the [sign convention](resolvent-sign-convention.md). See [resolvent analysis](modules/resolvent.md).

**Optimal energy gain.** The largest achievable energy ratio $\sigma_1^2 = \max_{f \neq 0} \|Hf\|_E^2 / \|f\|_F^2$: response energy in the Chu norm over forcing energy in the forcing norm. Computed as $\sigma = \sqrt{\mathrm{Re}(\lambda)}$ from the weighted normal eigenproblem, never from an explicit [SVD](https://grokipedia.com/page/Singular_value_decomposition) of $H$. "Optimal" means optimal over all forcing shapes at that $(\beta, \omega)$, not over frequencies.

**Forcing mode.** The optimal input shape $v$: the unit-norm vector attaining the leading gain. Normalized as $v^H W v = 1$ under the `chu` forcing norm or $v^H v = 1$ under `l2`. What to inject for maximum effect.

**Response mode.** The optimal output shape $u = Hv/\sigma$: what grows when the optimal forcing is applied. Always recovered by applying $H$, which is why the forward residual sits at roundoff by construction.

**Gain map.** Leading gains sampled over a $(\beta, \omega)$ grid: spanwise [wavenumber](https://grokipedia.com/page/Wavenumber) versus frequency. Peaks mark the flow's preferred amplifier settings. Production maps reuse anchor factorizations across nearby $\omega$ under a residual gate instead of refactoring per point. See [solver routing](modules/solvers.md).

**Discount ($\gamma$).** A real shift added as $(\gamma - i\omega) I - L_0$ with $\gamma > 0$ pushing poles off the imaginary axis. Keeps the shifted solve well posed near lightly damped eigenvalues. $\gamma = 0$ is the classical resolvent. Gains of a discounted resolvent answer the discounted question, so report $\gamma$ with the number.

**Nonnormality.** $L_0$ does not commute with its [adjoint](https://grokipedia.com/page/Adjoint) in the energy inner product ($H^H W \neq W H$ in the weighted sense). Consequence: all modes stable does not mean quiet. Quantitatively, with $\lambda_r$ the leading real part and $\kappa(V) = \|V\|\|V^{-1}\|$ the eigenvector conditioning, $\exp(2\tau\lambda_r) \le \|\exp(\tau L)\|^2 \le \kappa(V)\,\exp(2\tau\lambda_r)$: the upper bound is where transient growth lives, and it grows with nonnormality. (In repo convention $\lambda_r = \mathrm{Im}(\omega)$.) Mechanically, picture almost-colinear eigenvectors interfering constructively before decaying; the extreme is a non-diagonalizable Jordan block with algebraic growth. See Frantz, Loiseau and Robinet (2023), *Krylov methods for large-scale dynamical systems*, *Appl. Mech. Rev.* 75(3), 030802, non-modal stability. Nonnormal operators support large transient amplification, which is exactly what the gain map measures. The related spectral picture is the [pseudospectrum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudospectrum): $\{z : \|(zI - A)^{-1}\| > 1/\varepsilon\}$. Scholarpedia's [Stability](http://www.scholarpedia.org/article/Stability) article works the classic two-by-two transient-growth example.

**Optimal perturbation and transient growth.** The finite-time gain $\mathcal{G}(\tau) = \max_{x_0} \|\exp(\tau L)x_0\|^2/\|x_0\|^2$ equals $\sigma_1^2$, the squared leading singular value of the propagator; the maximizer is the first right singular vector and the response is $\sigma_1$ times the first left one. With the adjoint available this recasts as an eigenproblem rather than an SVD. Textbook illustration: plane Couette flow at $Re = 300$, linearly stable yet with optimal gain near 100, streamwise vortices growing into streaks. See Frantz, Loiseau and Robinet (2023), *Krylov methods for large-scale dynamical systems*, *Appl. Mech. Rev.* 75(3), 030802, non-modal stability and illustration.

**Receptivity.** The sensitivity of the flow to external disturbances: incoming noise, roughness, turbulence. Resolvent gains and [adjoint](https://grokipedia.com/page/Adjoint) modes quantify it. High gain at some $(\beta, \omega)$ means the environment can drive a large response there even when every eigenvalue is stable. Downstream of receptivity lies [transition to turbulence](http://www.scholarpedia.org/article/Transition_to_turbulence).


## Energy and adjoint vocabulary

**Chu energy norm.** The compressible disturbance-energy inner product. Diagonal in our discretization: $W = \tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathrm{diag}(W_\rho, W_u, W_v, W_w, W_T)$ built from quadrature weights, base density and temperature, $\kappa$, and Mach number (times radius in axisymmetric mode). Defines "large" for gains, mode normalization, and adjoints. A zero diagonal entry is a hard error at shell construction, not a warning.

**Adjoint mode.** An eigenvector of the energy-weighted adjoint $W^{-1} L_0^H W$. Where the direct mode shows what grows, the adjoint shows what the eigenvalue is sensitive to: the receptive shape. Returned in the temporal $\omega$ convention as conjugates of direct eigenvalues for real-valued base flows.

**Structural sensitivity (wavemaker).** The pointwise product of direct and adjoint mode magnitudes (Giannetti-Luchini). Marks where a localized structural tweak moves the eigenvalue most: the wavemaker region. The control-oriented output of running direct plus adjoint analysis together.


## Numerics vocabulary

**SBP operator.** A [summation-by-parts](https://grokipedia.com/page/Summation_by_parts) [finite-difference](https://grokipedia.com/page/Finite_difference_method) matrix: discrete derivative plus diagonal norm satisfying a discrete analogue of integration by parts, which bounds the discrete energy. Even interior orders 2, 4, 6, 8 only, each with validated boundary closures. Order 4 is the usual start.

**Sponge layer.** An artificial damping region near outflow and farfield boundaries that absorbs outgoing waves before they reflect. Implemented as a damping field added to the operator during assembly. Related idea, different mechanism: the [perfectly matched layer](https://grokipedia.com/page/Perfectly_matched_layer). A zero sponge array means no damping, which is valid for some cases and wrong for others; the baseflow plots show it.

**Boundary recipe.** The declarative list of [Dirichlet](https://grokipedia.com/page/Dirichlet_boundary_condition) and [Neumann](https://grokipedia.com/page/Neumann_boundary_condition) rules applied last in assembly: which borders, which variables, corner handling, curvilinear normals. Publishes the free degree-of-freedom sets every downstream solve must respect.

**BC penalty.** The number behind `bc: penalty:`. For Dirichlet rows, assembly zeroes the row and column, then writes `penalty` on the diagonal, so the constrained equation reads `penalty` times $q_i = 0$: the DOF is pinned to zero and decoupled from interior equations. In the temporal EVP (on $iL_0$) these pinned DOFs sit near $i \times$ `penalty`, far from physical targets, and the free-DOF sets plus acceptance checks keep them out of results. For Neumann rows, the normal-derivative stencil row is multiplied by `penalty`: the homogeneous constraint is unchanged, but the row is scaled to balance against interior rows in the factorization.

How to set it: keep the path default unless diagnostics complain. The driver and Song default to `1e8` (`bc.penalty` in YAML); assembly, the router, and the Martini examples default to `1e4` (nested `bc: penalty:` in their YAMLs, top-level `bc_penalty` or `penalty` in router dicts, `bc_penalty` kwarg in the direct API). Raise toward `1e6` (a validation case does exactly this) if constrained-Dirichlet leakage diagnostics show boundary modes leaking into results. Lower back down if you see conditioning trouble: a `1e8` diagonal next to order-1 interior entries is exactly the kind of scaling that can inflate residuals, and direct LU tolerates only so much.

**Artificial dissipation.** The term $-\varepsilon Q_{\mathrm{diss}}$ subtracted from $L_0$, with $Q_{\mathrm{diss}}$ the Mattsson-Svard-Nordstrom operator. Damps grid-scale sawtooth modes the centered SBP stencils admit. Two halves must both be set (build the operator, set the strength) or nothing happens silently. Off on rectilinear meshes, on for meshes curved in both directions. See the Workflow page.

**Implicit filter ($\alpha$).** The Mattsson-style spatial filter applied inside the resolvent masks and on the mesh. Strength parameter `alpha_filter`: $0.0$ is maximum filtering in the MATLAB convention, `"none"` disables. The adjoint path uses the adjoint-compliant variant so discrete adjointness holds.

**Spanwise wavenumber ($\beta$).** The real [wavenumber](https://grokipedia.com/page/Wavenumber) of the $e^{i\beta z}$ spanwise dependence. Enters the linearized physics, so each $\beta$ needs its own assembled $L_0$. $\beta = 0$ is the two-dimensional problem. Gain maps sweep $\beta$ on the outer loop.

**Floquet exponent.** The detuning parameter for spanwise-periodic [Floquet](https://grokipedia.com/page/Floquet_theory) analysis on streaky or modulated base flows. `continuum` is the default form; `matlab_parity` reproduces the LinStab2D algebra exactly for validation. Set per case, never guessed.

**Matrix dual path.** Operators assemble locally in SciPy CSC (from CSR blocks) and convert to PETSc AIJ for distributed solves, or assemble AIJ directly where supported. Layouts, backends, and the conversion bridge are defined in the [solver glossary](solver-glossary.md).


## Workflow vocabulary

**Shift target ($\sigma$).** The complex $\omega$-space point the eigensolver searches around. Lives in the YAML solver block, set explicitly on the spectral transformation. Near a branch it isolates modes cleanly; on a crowded real axis it returns mixtures. Moving slightly off-axis is a numerical search choice, not a physics change. Solver mechanics live in the [solver glossary](solver-glossary.md).

**Acceptance.** The postchecks a computed mode must pass before it is trusted: full-operator residual, boundary-condition leakage, target distance, spectral boxes, conjugate completeness. Converged Ritz pairs fail these regularly on interior non-Hermitian problems, which is why acceptance exists as a separate stage from convergence.

**Provenance.** The reproducibility record attached to every result: config hash, git SHA, backend and precision, mesh and norm settings. Stored inside the NPZ beside the numbers so a figure always traces back to the run that produced it.

## Beyond linear scope

Linear analysis predicts onset. What happens after onset is nonlinear and outside this repo, but two landmarks orient the map.

**Hopf bifurcation.** What happens after a mode goes unstable: an equilibrium sheds a limit cycle when a complex-conjugate eigenvalue pair crosses the imaginary axis. Linear analysis predicts the crossing ($\mathrm{Im}(\omega) = 0$ at criticality); the cycle itself needs the nonlinear terms. See [Scholarpedia: Andronov-Hopf bifurcation](http://www.scholarpedia.org/article/Andronov-Hopf_bifurcation) and [Bifurcation](http://www.scholarpedia.org/article/Bifurcation).

**Transition to turbulence.** The full path from laminar flow to turbulence: receptivity, linear amplification (modal or transient), secondary instability, breakdown. This repo covers the linear amplification step and the sensitivity fields around it. See [Scholarpedia: Transition to turbulence](http://www.scholarpedia.org/article/Transition_to_turbulence).

If a term appears elsewhere in this wiki without a definition or a link, that is a bug in that page. Link it here.

---

## FAQ

Source: https://linstabpy.vercel.app/faq/

# Frequently asked questions

Short answers to the questions new users actually ask, each pointing at the page with the full story. Conventions are fixed repo-wide: $\omega = \mathrm{eig}(i L_0)$, unstable exactly when $\mathrm{Im}(\omega) > 0$.

## Which analysis do I need?

**Temporal stability** if you ask "does the flow sustain self-excited disturbances" — growth rates and frequencies of global modes. **Spatial stability** if you prescribe a real frequency and ask how a disturbance grows downstream — the unknown is the complex streamwise wavenumber $\alpha$ from a quadratic-turned-generalized problem of twice the size. **Adjoint modes** if you ask "where is the flow receptive" — sensitivity and wavemaker fields from $W^{-1}L_0^H W$. **Resolvent** if you ask "which external forcing is amplified most" — optimal gains with forcing and response shapes at real $\omega$. Temporal, adjoint, and resolvent act on the same assembled $L_0$; spatial builds its own pencil from the same coefficients. Details in [core concepts](core-concepts.md), solver mechanics in the [solver glossary](solver-glossary.md).

## My spectrum moved when I changed the shift. Is that normal?

Yes, if you changed which branch the solver locked onto. Shift-invert finds eigenvalues near the target; on a crowded real axis, neighboring targets can return mixtures from different branches. Fix the branch first (small `nev`, a few nearby targets, compare postcheck residuals and target distances), then scale up. Moving the target slightly off the real axis often isolates a branch more cleanly. This is a numerical search choice, not a physics change. See [getting started](getting-started/index.md#your-first-own-case) and the paper's note that slow convergence near branches means widening the subspace or moving the shift.

## Do I turn the dissipation on?

Run the grid-scale leak test first: feed the operator a field alternating along one grid direction and constant along the other; a transverse derivative must return zero, so $\|D_x q\|/\|D_y q\|$ measures pure metric mixing. At round-off (the Song and Savarino meshes read below $10^{-11}$), the mesh is rectilinear: leave $\varepsilon = 0$ and confirm insensitivity under refinement. At order one (0.26 on one LES curved-wall mesh, 0.10–0.12 on a wavy-wall test), the mesh is bent: switch dissipation on and tune $\varepsilon$ on that mesh until the gain or eigenvalue stops moving. A value tuned elsewhere does not transfer. And remember the two halves: building the operator and setting the strength are separate flags, and setting only one is a silent no-op. Costs and the full procedure come from the paper's sawtooth section: $\varepsilon = 10^{-2}$ damps grid content at rate $\approx 0.3$ while resolved scales see $\varepsilon \times 10^{-2}$, for 15% more nonzeros and 3–4× wall time.

## My resolvent response shows point-to-point wiggles. What is that?

The odd–even (sawtooth) mode: the $q_i = (-1)^i$ family that every centered first-derivative stencil annihilates exactly, at any order. Only viscous terms damp it, at rate $\sim 1/(\mathrm{Re}\,h^2)$, so at high $\mathrm{Re}\,h^2$ it sits nearly neutral and whatever projects onto it stays. On rectilinear meshes it decouples and refinement removes it; on bent meshes the cross-metrics couple it into the resolved field and you need the dissipation from the previous answer. See the sawtooth discussion in [core concepts](core-concepts.md#numerics-vocabulary).

## What does `bc: penalty:` do, and what value?

Dirichlet rows are zeroed and the diagonal is set to `penalty`, pinning the DOF (`penalty`·$q_i = 0$); pinned modes land near $i \times$ `penalty`, far from physical targets. Neumann rows are scaled by it for row balance. Driver default `1e8`, library and router default `1e4`. Keep the default unless constrained-leakage diagnostics complain, then raise toward `1e6` first. Full mechanics in [core concepts](core-concepts.md#numerics-vocabulary).

## Why does `linstabpy run case.yaml` run the wrong case?

Because that command never existed. The CLI takes no case arguments — only `--version`. Case and output travel by `LINSTABPY_CASE_CONFIG` and `LINSTABPY_CASE_OUTPUT_NPZ`, and unknown bare words print a stderr warning but are otherwise ignored by design of the parser. See [getting started](getting-started/index.md#the-cli-as-it-really-is).

## Why did my run print `Cache valid` and finish instantly?

Rank 0 found an output NPZ whose stored config hash and git SHA match the current ones, so it skipped the compute. Point each run at its own output path, or export `LINSTABPY_FORCE_RECOMPUTE=1` deliberately. See [getting started](getting-started/index.md#the-cli-as-it-really-is).

## Which SBP order, and why only even ones?

Order 4 to start. Only even orders 2, 4, 6, 8 ship because only they have validated diagonal-norm boundary closures in this family. Higher order buys accuracy per point but stiffens the operator and grows stencils. See [core concepts](core-concepts.md#numerics-vocabulary).

## How big should `ncv` be?

Bigger than `nev`, then bigger again near branches. Measured guidance from the paper's campaign: on a 450k-unknown resolvent point, cutting the Krylov space from 20 vectors to 5 cut solves per point from 40 to 10 and moved the gain by less than $10^{-10}$ — subspace size sets cost, not precision, once past the threshold. If accepted-mode quality plateaus while the solve stays active, the subspace is too small for the neighborhood, not the tolerance too loose. Defaults per path live in the [solver glossary](solver-glossary.md#slepc-eps-eigensolvers-and-st-spectral-transformations).

## `nconv > 0`. Am I done?

No. Converged Ritz pairs can still fail full-operator residuals, boundary leakage, or target distance on interior non-Hermitian problems. Trust the acceptance postchecks, not the convergence count: requested `nev` vs converged `nconv`, explicit postcheck residuals, leakage diagnostics, and target distances for accepted and rejected modes alike. See [getting started](getting-started/index.md#your-first-own-case).

## Can I compare my gain with another paper's number?

Only if both weights match: response weight $W$ and forcing weight $W_f$. Kinetic-energy-only norms misrank compressible modes because thermodynamic fluctuations carry real energy share, and a Chu gain is simply not the same number as an $L^2$ gain. Always report forcing norm, response norm, $\beta$, $\omega$, $\gamma$, grid, and SBP order with the value. See [core concepts](core-concepts.md#resolvent-vocabulary).

## Direct or iterative linear solves?

Direct (`KSPPREONLY` + `PCLU` + MUMPS) unless memory says otherwise — it is the accuracy reference, and one factorization serves every iteration and every $H$/$H^H$ apply at that shift. Iterative paths (`fgmres_lu`, `strumpack_fgmres`) are explicit opt-ins for cases that do not fit direct factorization, always with `true_residual` on because transformed residuals can lie. The decision procedure with measured costs is in the [solver glossary](solver-glossary.md#choosing-a-configuration).

## One rank or many?

Factorization dominates (about four fifths of a resolvent point: 60 s factor vs 0.44 s solves and 5.8 s eigensolve at 450k unknowns), and it scales poorly: measured 190.5 s at 4 ranks, 154.6 s at 8, 148.2 s at 16, while peak memory doubled from 18.6 to 40.6 GiB. Start at 4 ranks with one thread each, compare on your machine, and scale out across cases (scheduler arrays) before scaling up ranks. Numbers from `examples/savarino/*.csv`; protocol in [getting started](getting-started/index.md#the-example-family-map).

## Where do I put a question this page does not answer?

Open an issue with the section that failed you, the command, the error, and the `--diagnose` output. Install problems especially — they are the most useful reports this project gets.

---

## Architecture

Source: https://linstabpy.vercel.app/architecture/

# Architecture

**LinStabPy** is a Python CLI and library for linear stability and resolvent analysis of compressible viscous flows. It ports LinStab2D linearized Navier-Stokes (LNSE) workflows from MATLAB to an MPI HPC stack on [PETSc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PETSc) and [SLEPc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SLEPc), with sparse direct factorization ([MUMPS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MUMPS_(software)) by default, optional [cuDSS](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cudss/)).

This page lists the packages and who owns which policy, the order in which a case runs, the stored data, and the quality gates. Package details are on the [module pages](modules/index.md).

!!! info "Conventions"
    Temporal [eigenvalues](https://grokipedia.com/page/Eigenvalues_and_eigenvectors) are $\omega = \mathrm{eig}(i L_0)$ with $\exp(-i\omega t)$ time dependence. Unstable means $\mathrm{Im}(\omega) > 0$. The shift-invert target lives in $\omega$ space. The [resolvent](https://grokipedia.com/page/Resolvent_formalism) is $H = C F ((\gamma - i\omega) I - L_0)^{-1} F B$ with $\sigma = \sqrt{\mathrm{Re}(\lambda)}$ from the weighted normal problem. [SBP](https://grokipedia.com/page/Summation_by_parts) orders are $2$, $4$, $6$, $8$ only. The default shifted solve is `KSPPREONLY` with `PCLU` through MUMPS, driven by SLEPc Krylov-Schur with `ST=SINVERT`. Assembly order is fixed: raw blocks, `inv(B/1j)` scaling, sponge, dissipation, then BC rows last. The state vector is $q = [\rho, u, v, w, T]$.


## Design rules

1. **Staged pipeline.** `driver/run.py` runs the stages in a fixed order: config, base flow, mesh, coefficients, $L_0$ with BCs, factorize, solve, payload. It records wall time and RSS per stage.
2. **One operator family.** Temporal, adjoint, spatial, single-frequency resolvent, and $\beta$-$\omega$ maps all consume BC-enforced LNSE operators. The spatial path reuses the temporal preparation helpers.
3. **Factorize once, solve many.** `linalg.factorize` is shared by shift-invert eigenproblems and by every $H$ and $H^H$ apply at one shift.
4. **Config is the single policy source.** YAML, then environment, then defaults, then schema validation into typed `Config` subsections. Invalid structure or FD orders fail before any factorization.
5. **Lazy imports.** `import linstabpy` and the package, mesh, BC, linalg, stability, resolvent, and router packages resolve names through PEP 562 `__getattr__`. PETSc and MPI start only on solve paths. Importing `driver.run` is the intentional boundary.
6. **SciPy and PETSc paths.** Local assembly uses SciPy CSC/CSR. The production path converts to distributed PETSc `Mat` through `utils/petsc_core.py`, which keeps mesh and solver packages independent.
7. **Declarative BCs and cost-aware routing.** Case behavior comes from YAML and BC rules. The router decides between reuse and refactor from measured factor cost, memory, and residuals.
8. **Reproducibility.** Config hash, git SHA, a metrics schema, and fixed NPZ contract keys.

The layers, from the entry point down: orchestration, analysis domains, discretization and operators, linear algebra, utilities.

| Layer | Choice |
|-------|--------|
| Language | Python 3.11 to 3.14 |
| Local arrays and sparse | NumPy, SciPy (CSC/CSR) |
| Parallel runtime | MPI via `mpi4py` |
| Distributed linear algebra | PETSc (`petsc4py`), complex scalars required |
| Eigenproblems | SLEPc (`slepc4py`), EPS and weighted normal problems |
| Sparse direct solvers | MUMPS through `PCLU` (default); optional cuDSS as a GPU shell PC |
| Configuration | PyYAML, typed dataclasses, schema validation |
| Outputs | NPZ result payloads, `metrics.json`, provenance |

`environment.yml` targets conda-forge complex-scalar PETSc/SLEPc. GPU PETSc is not a supported conda path; cuDSS is an optional, non-conda path.


## Packages

```text
src/linstabpy/
├── __init__.py              # Lazy public API (no PETSc on import)
├── metrics_schema.py        # Run metrics JSON contract
├── mumps_options.py         # MUMPS option helpers
├── driver/                  # CLI + case pipeline
├── config/                  # Schema, typed Config, defaults
├── baseflow/                # BaseFlow + I/O + preprocess
├── mesh/                    # Mesh, SBP, filters, FD weights
├── operators/               # LNSE assembly, coefficients, spatial, norms
├── boundary_conditions/     # Dirichlet/Neumann recipes
├── stability/               # Eigenvalue services, acceptance, sensitivity
├── resolvent/               # Operator, gain, analysis
├── solvers/                 # EPS backends + router/
├── linalg/                  # factorize, backends, shifted, cuDSS
└── utils/                   # PETSc init/core, YAML, metrics, provenance
```

| Package | Code paths | Role | Page |
|---------|------------|------|------|
| Case orchestration | `driver/`, `__init__.py` | PETSc/MPI init, staged runs, CLI, payload, public lazy API | [Runtime driver](modules/driver.md) |
| Configuration | `config/` | Merge and validate YAML, env, defaults; typed solver policy | [Configuration](modules/config.md) |
| Base flow | `baseflow/` | Mean-flow ingest, sponge, shock cleanup, viscosity | [Base flow](modules/baseflow.md) |
| Mesh | `mesh/` | Geometry, SBP operators, filters, deformation, masking | [Structured mesh](modules/mesh.md) |
| LNSE assembly | `operators/`, `boundary_conditions/` | Coefficients, $L_0$ and spatial assembly, BC recipes, Chu norm | [LNSE assembly](modules/operators.md), [BC recipes](modules/boundary-conditions.md) |
| Stability | `stability/`, `solvers/eigenvalue.py`, `solvers/spatial_eig.py` | Temporal, adjoint, and spatial EPS, sensitivity | [Stability analysis](modules/stability.md) |
| Resolvent | `resolvent/` | $H$ operator, weighted gains, forcing models | [Resolvent analysis](modules/resolvent.md) |
| Solver routing | `solvers/router/` | $\beta$-$\omega$ maps, anchors, residual gates, RAM autoselect | [Solvers and routing](modules/solvers.md) |
| Linear algebra | `linalg/`, `mumps_options.py` | Factor backends, shifted operators, cuDSS | [Linear algebra](modules/linalg.md) |
| Shared utilities | `utils/`, `metrics_schema.py` | PETSc bridge, YAML, cost, provenance, Floquet | [Shared utilities](modules/shared-utilities.md) |

`boundary_conditions/` is a separate package for import hygiene and MATLAB module parity. Functionally it belongs to LNSE assembly: BC application is the last step of operator finalization.

Public library surface (lazy exports from `linstabpy.__init__`): `build_lnse_system`, `build_lnse_operator`, `compute_chu_norm`, `temporal_eigenvalues`, `adjoint_eigenvalues`, `wavemaker`, `resolvent_analysis`, `resolvent_map`, `BaseFlow`. The CLI entry is `linstabpy.driver.cli.main`, which imports `driver.run` only after handling `--version` and `--help`.

Calls between packages are in-process Python calls:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  CO["Case orchestration"]
  CM["Configuration"]
  BM["Base flow"]
  MD["Mesh"]
  OA["LNSE assembly + BC"]
  SA["Stability"]
  RA["Resolvent"]
  RR["Router"]
  LI["Linear algebra"]
  UT["Utilities"]

  CO --> CM
  CO --> BM
  CO --> SA
  CO --> RA
  CO --> RR
  CO --> OA
  CO --> LI
  OA --> MD
  OA --> BM
  OA --> LI
  SA --> LI
  SA --> OA
  RA --> LI
  RA --> OA
  RR --> RA
  RR --> LI
  RR --> OA
  BM --> MD
  MD --> UT
  SA --> UT
  RA --> UT
  LI --> UT
```

Library consumers may call assembly and analysis APIs directly and skip the driver. They still depend on the same operator and factorization contracts. Stability and resolvent never own mesh generation; they consume finished operators and energy weights. Utilities never own case flow.


## Ownership

Keep policy in the owning module rather than recreating pass-through files.

| Area | Owning module | What belongs there |
|---|---|---|
| Boundary-condition recipes | `linstabpy.boundary_conditions.recipe` | YAML recipe parsing, rule validation, effective rows, column-zeroed Dirichlet rows, overlap reporting, and SciPy/PETSc/spatial dispatch. |
| LNSE assembly | `linstabpy.operators.assembly` | Coefficient preparation, backend choice, operator construction order, boundary-condition application, and the `LNSESystem` result object. |
| Solver policy | `linstabpy.utils._solver_cfg`, `linstabpy.config.typed` | Dict/env resolution, PETSc/SLEPc defaults, MUMPS/KSP/EPS setup, and resolvent linear-solver selection. |
| Runtime pipeline | `linstabpy.driver.run` | Case loading, mesh construction, Chu norm, assembly, stability/resolvent stages, postchecks, acceptance, and `.npz` persistence. |
| Packed-field ingest | `linstabpy.baseflow.grid_fields` | One loader for npz or an npy directory. Filter, boundary sponge, and shock live in `baseflow.preprocess`. |
| Result archive | `linstabpy.driver.payload`, `linstabpy.driver.io` | Payload grouping and NPZ/sidecar write. `io.py` does not import the driver. |
| Mesh state | `linstabpy.mesh.mesh` | Structured geometry, derivative operators, filters, dissipation state, and sponge state. |

Rules that go with the table:

- **Boundary conditions.** `BCRecipe` is the seam. Public YAML files pass lists of dictionaries; the recipe layer normalizes them. When changing BC behavior, update the recipe analysis and every backend wrapper together. Do not duplicate row-selection logic in assembly, runtime code, or example scripts.
- **LNSE assembly.** `LNSESystem` is the assembly handoff. The construction order is part of the numerical contract: prepare coefficients, build the raw operator, apply the inverse mass/metric block, apply sponge and operator dissipation, then apply boundary conditions. Keep this order explicit in `operators.assembly`. Runtime callers ask for an assembled system and do not rebuild pieces of the sequence.
- **Solver policy.** `Config` in `config.typed` reads YAML and environment variables. PETSc/SLEPc objects are created inside the solver modules, but defaults and fallbacks come from the shared policy layer. The launcher, `mpi4py`, PETSc, and SLEPc must agree on one MPI stack; installer checks report the chosen stack.
- **Dissipation.** Every path, the map router included, reads dissipation from `numerics.operator_dissipation` through `config.defaults.stage_dissipation_epsilon`. The old top-level `dissipation_epsilon` and `eps_resolv` keys are refused.
- **Mesh state.** `Mesh` is the main structured-grid object. Deformation and masking must preserve numerical behavior. A geometry-only optimization is allowed only when tests show that derivative operators, filters, weights, and saved outputs stay equivalent for the relevant cases.
- **Packed fields.** Every packed case uses the same eight keys: `x`, `y`, `rho`, `u`, `v`, `w`, `T`, `sponge`. YAML names the file; the loader does not guess a Song filename. Martini `.mat` constructors live in `examples/linstab2d/matlab_baseflow.py`.
- **Runtime and NPZ output.** Example scripts set `LINSTABPY_CASE_CONFIG` and call `linstabpy.driver.run`. Martini generated-mesh examples build their own fields; packed-field cases go through `load_case_fields`. The compatibility surface for saved results is `RUNTIME_NPZ_CONTRACT_KEYS` in `linstabpy.driver.payload`; the grouped explanation is the [runtime NPZ contract](development/runtime-npz-contract.md) page. Additive fields are acceptable. Renames or removals need a migration note, test updates, and reader updates.


## Run order

Every analysis product shares the preparation stages. Step 7 is where the paths split.

| Step | Operation | Inputs | Outputs | Code |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Runtime init: `init_petsc_from_argv()`, then MPI/PETSc imports; config path from `LINSTABPY_CASE_CONFIG` (required) | argv, env | PETSc/MPI ready, rank-0 logging | `driver/run.py` |
| 2 | Config merge and schema validation | YAML, env, defaults | Typed `Config`, or `ConfigValidationError` | `config/schema.py`, `config/typed.py` |
| 3 | Field I/O | npy directory or npz | Dict of 2-D float fields | `baseflow/grid_fields.py` |
| 4 | Preprocess and transport | Raw primitives | `BaseFlow` with mu and sponge | `baseflow/preprocess.py`, `sponge.py`, `viscosity.py` |
| 5 | Mesh and SBP | x, y, FD order, deformation | `Mesh` with operators and runtime state | `mesh/mesh.py`, `mesh/sbp.py` |
| 6 | Coefficients | `BaseFlow`, metrics | Cartesian or cylindrical LNSE coefficient blocks | `operators/coefficients.py` |
| 7 | $L_0$ finalization and BC recipes | Coefficients, FD matrices, sponge, backend request | SciPy CSC or PETSc `Mat` $L_0$, free-DOF sets | `operators/assembly.py`, `boundary_conditions/` |
| 8 | Factorization | Shifted $L_0$ | `Factorization` handle | `linalg/factorize.py` |
| 9 | Solve: SLEPc EPS or weighted normal shell | Factor, weights | Eigenvalues, modes, gains | `stability/`, `resolvent/`, `solvers/` |
| 10 | Postcheck and acceptance | Modes, residuals | Accepted modes, advisories | `stability/acceptance.py`, `driver/preflight.py` |
| 11 | Payload | Results, cost, provenance | NPZ and `metrics.json` | `driver/payload.py`, `driver/io.py` |

State progression: raw files, validated config, `BaseFlow` on `(ny, nx)`, mesh runtime state, coefficient tensors, constrained sparse $L_0$ with free-DOF mask, factor, solution, accepted result, emitted payload.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
  subgraph Entry
    A1["CLI: linstabpy.driver.cli"]
    A2["Library: import linstabpy"]
  end

  subgraph Pipeline["Staged pipeline"]
    direction TB
    P1["Config validate + typed policy"]
    P2["Base flow load + preprocess"]
    P3["Mesh + SBP + filters"]
    P4["Coefficients + L0 + BC"]
    P5["Factorize shifted systems"]
    P6a["Stability EPS"]
    P6b["Resolvent H / gains"]
    P6c["Router beta-omega map"]
    P7["NPZ + metrics + provenance"]
    P1 --> P2 --> P3 --> P4 --> P5
    P5 --> P6a
    P5 --> P6b
    P4 --> P6c
    P6c --> P6b
    P6a --> P7
    P6b --> P7
    P6c --> P7
  end

  A1 --> P1
  A2 --> P4
  A2 --> P6a
  A2 --> P6b
  A2 --> P6c
```

Two entry paths converge on the same operator core and factorization layer. The CLI and driver path (`driver/run.py`) initializes PETSc/MPI, resolves config, logs stages and heartbeats, and writes the payload. The library path (`import linstabpy`) starts nothing on import and loads public symbols on first use.

### Temporal eigenvalues (primary product)

Steps 1 to 8 above, then:

- **Shift-invert factorization.** `linalg/factorize.py` factorizes with the backend chosen by `resolve_factor_backend` and the MUMPS options. The default is `KSPPREONLY` + `PCLU` + MUMPS. Iterative solves are an explicit opt-in for memory-bound cases, not a silent fallback. The API is solve, transpose solve, block solve, refactorize, destroy.
- **Eigenanalysis.** SLEPc EPS through `stability/_eigenvalues.py` and `solvers/eigenvalue.py`. EPS iterations call repeated solves against the factor. Post-processing: residual norms and reordering, target-distance check, conjugate-pair completeness, `stability/acceptance.py`.
- **Output.** `build_runtime_payload` packs eigenvalues, eigenvectors, metrics, and provenance. The NPZ path comes from the environment or defaults to `{prefix}_{config_md5}_{git_sha8}.npz`.

### Adjoint and structural sensitivity

`adjoint_eigenvalues` (lazy export from `stability._eigenvalues`) runs the adjoint solve after the direct modes exist. `wavemaker` in `stability/sensitivity.py` combines direct and adjoint modes. The factorization layer provides the transpose solves the adjoint needs.

### Resolvent gain (single frequency)

The preparation matches the temporal path. Then:

1. Factor $((\gamma - i\omega) I - L_0)$ once. Under `solver.resolvent_sign_convention: matlab_parity` the code inverts the older LinStab2D matrix instead; see the [resolvent sign convention](resolvent-sign-convention.md).
2. Apply $H$ and $H^H$ through the factor: input map $B$, solve, output map $C$ (`resolvent/operator.py`). `compute_chu_norm` supplies the energy weights.
3. Build the weighted normal operator `invW * H^H * W * H(v)` as a PETSc `MatShell` (`resolvent/gain.py`).
4. Run SLEPc on the shell, validate residuals, and return gains with forcing and response modes (`resolvent/analysis.py`).

### Gain map over $\beta$ and $\omega$

Entry: `solvers/router/resolvent_map.py` (public `resolvent_map`).

1. **Per-$\beta$ assembly.** One BC-enforced operator per spanwise wavenumber.
2. **Band marking.** `band_marking.py` labels frequency bands NEAR_POLE, SMOOTH, or STABLE to choose the walk strategy.
3. **Line walk.** `map_walk.LineWalker` pays a real factor for the first frequencies on a line and records factor time, memory, and compression. Later points apply $K(\omega)^{-1}$ with that factor as a right preconditioner. A residual gate forces a new factor when accuracy degrades; a walk may be deferred (`WalkDeferred`) or aborted.
4. **Stable-regime sweeps.** `stable_sweep.py` runs anchor-preconditioned sweeps across nearby frequencies.
5. **Backend policy.** `linalg/backends.py` normalizes and probes MUMPS, LU, and cuDSS. RAM autoselect and break-even logic influence the choice.
6. **Leading gain.** Computed by the resolvent analysis at each scheduled point.
7. **Recording.** Map arrays, cost keys (wall assemble/factor/solve, peak RSS and GPU memory, ranks, git SHA), and certification metadata. `map_record` saves atomically.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    WalkInit["LineWalker start band"]
    PayAnchor["Factor true operator at anchor omega"]
    MeasureCost["Record factor time memory compression"]
    NextOm["Next frequency"]
    PCApply["Use anchor factor as right PC"]
    SolveOm["Solve shifted system gain EPS"]
    Gate{"Residual below threshold?"}
    Keep["Accept gain continue"]
    NewFac["New real factor become anchor"]
    Done{"Line complete?"}
    WalkEnd["Return samples reasons"]

    WalkInit --> PayAnchor
    PayAnchor --> MeasureCost
    MeasureCost --> NextOm
    NextOm --> PCApply
    PCApply --> SolveOm
    SolveOm --> Gate
    Gate -->|Yes| Keep
    Gate -->|No| NewFac
    NewFac --> MeasureCost
    Keep --> Done
    Done -->|No| NextOm
    Done -->|Yes| WalkEnd
```

Dissipation depends on the mesh. On rectilinear tensor meshes the metric cross-terms vanish, so dissipation can be a costly no-op for gain accuracy. On meshes curvilinear in both directions, an undamped operator can show spurious near-singular resonances. Enable it in pairs: `enabled` builds $Q_{\mathrm{diss}}$ on the mesh and `epsilon` is the strength.

The outer loop is $\beta$ and the inner loop is the frequency line. Each point ends in one of: continue, refactor, defer, abort. Walks on one line stay sequential to preserve factor reuse; parallelism across $\beta$ lines is not implemented.

### Spatial eigenproblem

- **Config.** `solver.spatial`, with fallback to `solver.eigen` when no spatial YAML section exists.
- **Assembly.** `operators/spatial.py` reuses the temporal preparation and index helpers, with SciPy and PETSc block-matrix paths.
- **Solve.** `solvers/spatial_eig.py` runs a generalized SLEPc EPS with a direct shift-invert backend chosen as for the temporal case. Output: spatial eigenvalues, modes, and solver metadata.


## Stored data

LinStabPy is file-oriented. There is no database; reproducibility comes from config hashing, schema versions, and fixed result contracts.

| Store | Form | Contract |
|-------|------|----------|
| Case policy | YAML on disk, env overrides | Merged into typed `Config`; schema-validated |
| Mean flow | npy directory or npz | Primitives `RHO,U,V,W,T` on `(ny,nx)`; optional sponge |
| Runtime operators | In-memory SciPy CSC or PETSc `Mat` | Sparse $5 N_{gp} \times 5 N_{gp}$, or reduced free DOFs |
| Results | NPZ | Fixed key contract in `driver.payload` |
| Metrics | JSON | `metrics_schema.SCHEMA`: provenance, problem, cost, quality |
| Provenance | Embedded in metrics and payload | Config hash/MD5, git SHA, hostname, factor backend and precision |

```text
YAML + npy/npz
    → Config (typed) + BaseFlow (ny,nx fields)
    → Mesh (X,Y, Dx,Dy, W, filters)
    → Coefficients + Energy weights (Chu W_diag / invW_diag)
    → L0 PETSc Mat + free-DOF IS + BC-enforced rows
    → Factorization handle(s)
    → Spectra / gains / modes (distributed Vec → gathered arrays)
    → NPZ payload + metrics.json (provenance, cost, quality)
```

| Object | Contract |
|--------|----------|
| `BaseFlow` | Parameters (`Re,Ma,Pr,kappa,T_0`) and `(ny,nx)` primitives; optional MU and dmu/dT |
| `Mesh` and operators | `X,Y`, SBP `Dx,Dy,...`, weights `W`, optional dissipation |
| `LNSESystem` ($L_0$) | Sparse, size scale `5 * ngp`, or reduced free DOFs |
| BC recipe | Rules, enforced rows, free-DOF index sets |
| Energy weights | Chu norm diagonals `W_diag` and `invW_diag` |
| Factors | Opaque `Factorization` handle that owns the KSP/PC lifecycle |
| Modes and gains | Distributed `Vec`, gathered to NumPy for the payload |
| Map records | Structured arrays, cost samples, certification |

`driver/run.py` is about 1.8k lines and owns stage sequencing, timing, and payload emission. One place defines "a case", which helps reproducibility but raises change risk. Library users can bypass it.


## Runtime behavior

- **Logging.** Rank 0 writes the human-readable log. Stage lines are machine-parseable: `stage complete: stage=<name> elapsed=<s> rss_peak_delta_bytes=<n>`. Heartbeats default to every 30 s (`LINSTABPY_STAGE_HEARTBEAT_SECONDS`).
- **Environment.** `LINSTABPY_CASE_CONFIG`, `LINSTABPY_CASE_OUTPUT_NPZ`, `LINSTABPY_FORCE_RECOMPUTE`, and the log prefix. Use a dedicated output NPZ per concurrent run.
- **Cache.** The CLI reuses an NPZ when config hash and git SHA match, unless `LINSTABPY_FORCE_RECOMPUTE` is set.
- **MPI.** PETSc `COMM_WORLD` ranks share distributed matrices and vectors. One MPI job runs one case or one map campaign. There is no server process.
- **Init order.** Initialize `mpi4py` before PETSc, with thread level MULTIPLE when a backend requires it. `import linstabpy` alone does not set up the parallel runtime.
- **Requirements.** Python 3.11 to 3.14, working MPI with `mpi4py`, complex-scalar PETSc/SLEPc, MUMPS through PETSc, NumPy, SciPy, PyYAML. cuDSS is optional. Large cases are memory-bound by the sparse factors.
- **Factor lifecycle.** Create, solve N times, refactorize (same nonzero pattern), destroy.


## Quality gates and errors

| Gate | Behavior |
|------|----------|
| Schema validation | Unknown top-level keys and invalid FD orders raise `ConfigValidationError` before any mesh or factor work |
| Base flow I/O | Missing field names or non-2-D arrays raise at load |
| BC recipe | Invalid symbols or inconsistent borders and variables fail in recipe analysis and application |
| Backend availability | A requested MUMPS, LU, or cuDSS backend that is not present fails in the probe in `backends.py`, before factorization |
| Factorization | PETSc, MUMPS, and STRUMPACK failures raise dedicated errors and destroy partial state |
| Refactorize | A changed nonzero pattern raises `NotImplementedError` or a PETSc error |
| Preflight advisories | Non-blocking warnings (dissipation versus mesh coupling, freestream scale); the run continues |
| Eigen quality | Residual norms, target distance, conjugate-pair completeness (`stability/acceptance.py`) before the payload is written |
| Resolvent and map quality | Residual gate forces a refactor when preconditioner reuse loses accuracy; reason codes OK, PENDING, FAILED per point |
| Certification | Router consistency and RSVD-style certification metadata |

Principles:

- Fail fast on reproducibility gates (config, missing backends) rather than run expensive wrong physics.
- Refactor rather than return inaccurate gains from a failed residual gate.
- Iterative linear solvers are never an automatic downgrade from direct factors. They need an explicit solver policy.
- A gain map records completed $(\beta, \omega)$ cells with FAILED or PENDING markers when one line breaks, instead of discarding the campaign.
- On a STRUMPACK or MUMPS failure, check the backend build, the matrix conditioning and BC setup, and memory. Retrying without a config change does not help.


## Troubleshooting map

| Symptom | Likely stage | First checks |
|---|---|---|
| Immediate abort | Config or schema | YAML keys, FD orders |
| Bad spectra or gains | Base flow, BC, assembly | Field alignment, BC recipe, sponge |
| Factor crash or out of memory | Linear algebra | Backend probe, ranks, BLR, iterative opt-in |
| Noisy map ridges | Router and mesh dissipation | Metric cross-coupling, dissipation `enabled` and `epsilon` set together |
| Slow dense $\omega$ grid | Map walk | Anchor spacing, residual threshold, stable sweep |

On map jobs, compare `cost_wall_factor_s` with `cost_wall_solve_s` and watch the residual-driven refactor rate. See [Troubleshooting](troubleshooting.md) for install and runtime problems.
