## Solver glossary

Source: https://linstabpy.vercel.app/solver-glossary/

# PETSc and SLEPc glossary

Definitions of every solver term used in this wiki, linked to the official docs. Assumes linear algebra ([Krylov](https://grokipedia.com/page/Krylov_subspace) subspaces, [LU](https://grokipedia.com/page/LU_decomposition), [eigenvalues](https://grokipedia.com/page/Eigenvalues_and_eigenvectors)) No prior PETSc or SLEPc experience needed. Readers who already use PETSc can skip to [The exact chains this repo runs](#the-exact-chains-this-repo-runs).

**The two libraries.** [PETSc](https://petsc.org/release/manual/ksp/) (Portable, Extensible Toolkit for Scientific Computation) owns distributed vectors and matrices plus linear solvers. [SLEPc](https://slepc.upv.es/documentation/current/docs/manualpages/EPS/EPSSetProblemType/) (Scalable Library for Eigenvalue Problem Computations) sits on top of PETSc and owns eigensolvers. LinStabPy drives both through their Python bindings, [petsc4py](https://petsc4py.readthedocs.io/en/stable/) and [slepc4py](https://slepc4py.readthedocs.io/en/stable/), over [mpi4py](https://mpi4py.readthedocs.io/) for [MPI](https://grokipedia.com/page/Message_Passing_Interface). The install guide explains how to build this stack. This page explains what the objects mean. Physics and math vocabulary (growth rate, gain, Chu norm, wavemaker) lives in the [core concepts](core-concepts.md) companion.

Repo conventions used below: $\omega = \mathrm{eig}(i L_0)$, unstable exactly when $\mathrm{Im}(\omega) > 0$; [resolvent](https://grokipedia.com/page/Resolvent_formalism) $H = C F ((\gamma - i\omega) I - L_0)^{-1} F B$.


## Mental model

Four object pairs cover nearly everything:

| Pair | Library | Job in one line |
|---|---|---|
| [`Mat`](https://petsc.org/release/manualpages/Mat/Mat/) and [`Vec`](https://petsc.org/release/manualpages/Vec/Vec/) | PETSc | A sparse matrix and a vector, distributed across MPI ranks. |
| [`KSP`](https://petsc.org/release/manual/ksp/) and [`PC`](https://petsc.org/release/manual/ksp/) | PETSc | A linear solver (`KSP`) split from its preconditioner (`PC`), so any iteration can pair with any preconditioner. |
| [`EPS`](https://slepc.upv.es/documentation/current/docs/manualpages/EPS/EPSSetProblemType/) and [`ST`](https://slepc.upv.es/documentation/current/docs/manualpages/ST/STSetShift/) | SLEPc | An eigensolver (`EPS`) split from its spectral transformation (`ST`), so any eigensolver can pair with shift-invert. |
| Shell matrices | PETSc | A `Mat` you never assemble. You provide the multiply function and PETSc calls it. |

A typical LinStabPy solve wires all four: a distributed `Mat` holds the shifted operator, a `KSP` with `PC` factors it once, an `EPS` with `ST` runs shift-invert Krylov-Schur calling that factor on every iteration, and the resolvent path adds a shell matrix whose multiply applies $H$ through the same factor.


## PETSc basics

**PETSc** is a C library (with Python bindings) for vectors, matrices, and solvers on distributed memory. Start with the [KSP manual chapter](https://petsc.org/release/manual/ksp/). It covers linear solves end to end and is the best single document behind this page.

**Communicators.** Every PETSc object lives on an MPI communicator, almost always `COMM_WORLD` here. Ranks own disjoint row ranges of each matrix and vector. Only the owning rank writes its range. When the docs say "rank 0 owns logging and IO decisions," that is convention in our driver, not a PETSc requirement.

**[`Mat`](https://petsc.org/release/manualpages/Mat/Mat/) and [`Vec`](https://petsc.org/release/manualpages/Vec/Vec/).** The distributed matrix and vector types. The default [sparse](https://grokipedia.com/page/Sparse_matrix) CPU format is AIJ (compressed sparse row across ranks). LinStabPy assembles locally in SciPy CSC or CSR, then converts to a distributed `Mat` in `utils/petsc_core.py`. Sizes here are $5$ unknowns per grid point before boundary elimination, so a $300 \times 100$ grid gives a $150{,}000 \times 150{,}000$ complex sparse matrix.

**SciPy CSC and CSR.** The two compressed formats from [`scipy.sparse`](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/sparse.html) (background: [sparse matrix](https://grokipedia.com/page/Sparse_matrix)). CSR stores row by row: values plus column indices plus row-start pointers. CSC stores the transpose pattern: values plus row indices plus column-start pointers. Same entries, different access direction. Assembly here builds small blocks in CSR and finalizes the full $L_0$ as complex CSC. Both convert to each other freely, and every solver entry point accepts either; the bridge normalizes to CSR on the way into PETSc.

**PETSc AIJ.** PETSc's sparse format: a distributed CSR. Each rank owns a contiguous row range and stores its rows as `(indptr, indices, data)` triples, created via `Mat().createAIJ(size, csr, comm)`. Two layouts exist. *Local* AIJ on `COMM_SELF` holds the whole matrix on one rank (single-rank style). *Distributed* AIJ on `COMM_WORLD` splits rows across ranks by ownership ranges. Same object type, different communicator and row distribution.

**The bridge (`utils/petsc_core.py`).** One module owns every conversion so call sites never hand-roll them:

| Function | Job |
|---|---|
| `scipy_to_petsc` | SciPy matrix to PETSc AIJ `Mat`. Layout follows `petsc_matrix_mode` (below). |
| `scipy_to_petsc_distributed`, `scipy_to_petsc_distributed_from_root` | Ownership-aware distributed AIJ, scattering rows to owner ranks. |
| `petsc_to_scipy` | PETSc `Mat` back to SciPy (`csr` or `csc`). Used for comparison, parity, and SciPy-only paths. |
| `create_distributed_aij`, `insert_local_csr_rows`, `assemble_matrix` | Lower-level distributed construction used inside assembly and conversion. |
| `ownership_range`, `petsc_owned_rows` | Which global rows this rank owns, and their CSR data. |
| `require_complex` | Asserts complex-scalar PETSc and installs one-time MUMPS defaults. Fails fast otherwise. |
| `compare_sparse_matrices`, `compare_petsc_against_scipy`, `petsc_matvec_residual` | Parity helpers proving the two paths hold the same operator. |

**`assembly_backend`: where $L_0$ gets built.** YAML or `LINSTABPY_ASSEMBLY_BACKEND`, default `scipy`. `scipy` assembles CSC locally and converts on demand: the cross-machine baseline, and mandatory for adjoint workflows (`adjoint_eigenvalues` rejects PETSc matrices today). `petsc` assembles AIJ directly, but with two documented limits: direct PETSc assembly cannot apply `dissipation_epsilon`, and distributed direct assembly covers model `2D` only. When in doubt, SciPy-assemble then convert.

**`petsc_matrix_mode`: local or distributed AIJ.** YAML or `LINSTABPY_PETSC_MATRIX_MODE`, default `auto`. `local` and `serial` force single-rank AIJ. `distributed`, `mpi`, and `parallel` force ownership-split AIJ. `auto` picks distributed exactly when the MPI world has more than one rank (and local when PETSc is absent). Anything else raises `ValueError` naming the valid words.

**Rule of thumb.** Small cases, debugging, adjoint work, and MATLAB parity: `scipy` backend with local matrices. Production MPI runs: same SciPy assembly, converted to distributed AIJ for the factorize and eigensolve stages. The operator values are identical either way; only the layout changes.

**Complex scalars.** PETSc compiles for either real or complex floating point, chosen at build time. This repo requires complex builds: eigenvalues, shifts, and modes are complex throughout. `install.sh --check` asserts this. A real-scalar PETSc imports fine and then fails real work, which is why the check exists.

**Init order.** Import `mpi4py` before `petsc4py` so MPI initializes with thread level `MULTIPLE`, which some factor backends need. Plain `import linstabpy` initializes neither. The driver and solver modules initialize them when a solve stage starts. Solver modules that need SLEPc call the shared init helper first.

**Options database.** PETSc and SLEPc read command-line style options at runtime (`-ksp_type`, `-eps_monitor`, and hundreds more). Any example can receive them after `--` through the runner, for example `-- -eps_monitor` to watch eigensolver convergence. YAML and env policy in this repo set the important ones explicitly, but the options database is always available as an override and debugging channel.


## KSP: linear solvers and the PREONLY direct path

**[`KSP`](https://petsc.org/release/manual/ksp/)** (Krylov Subspace Solver) is PETSc's linear solver object: given $Ax = b$, it produces $x$. The key design point is the split: `KSP` chooses the *iteration* (or none), [`PC`](https://petsc.org/release/manual/ksp/) chooses the *[preconditioner](https://grokipedia.com/page/Preconditioner)*. You can pair [GMRES](https://grokipedia.com/page/Generalized_minimal_residual_method) with LU, or no iteration with LU, without touching calling code. SLEPc shift-invert and our resolvent applies both consume `KSP` objects through this interface.

**[`KSPPREONLY`](https://petsc.org/release/manualpages/KSP/KSPPREONLY/)** means: no Krylov iteration at all, just apply the preconditioner once. When the preconditioner is an exact LU factorization, that single apply *is* the direct solve. This is why our default shifted solve is described as "`KSPPREONLY` with `PCLU` through [MUMPS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MUMPS_(software))": mathematically it is sparse direct LU, reached through the `KSP` interface so every consumer (eigen shift-invert, resolvent applies, transpose solves) shares one code path. Stated in `linalg/factorize.py`: the default path is `KSPPREONLY` + `PCLU` + MUMPS.

**[`KSPGMRES`](https://petsc.org/release/manualpages/KSP/KSPGMRES/)** is restarted GMRES, the standard Krylov method for nonsymmetric systems. GMRES builds an orthogonal basis of the Krylov subspace and minimizes the residual over it, restarting every *restart* steps to bound memory (default 50 in our router). This repo uses GMRES in exactly one place: the $\beta$ and $\omega$ map router reuses an anchor factorization as a right preconditioner for nearby frequencies, solving each nearby system with right-preconditioned GMRES (restart 50, max 200 iterations) until a residual gate forces a fresh factorization. See the Solver Routing page.

**[`KSPFGMRES`](https://petsc.org/release/manualpages/KSP/KSPFGMRES/)** is flexible GMRES, which tolerates a preconditioner that changes between iterations (for example an inner iterative solve). Ours uses it on two explicit opt-in paths: `fgmres_lu` (FGMRES around an LU preconditioner) and `strumpack_fgmres` (FGMRES around a [STRUMPACK](https://portal.nersc.gov/project/sparse/strumpack/) approximate factor), plus the [cuDSS](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cudss/) GPU path where the GPU factor preconditions an FGMRES outer iteration. Iterative paths are never silent fallback here. They require explicit solver policy.

**[`KSPSetTolerances`](https://petsc.org/release/manualpages/KSP/KSPSetTolerances/)** sets relative tolerance, absolute tolerance, divergence tolerance, and maximum iterations for the Krylov iteration. On the default `KSPPREONLY` path these knobs do nothing, because there is no iteration. Accuracy there comes from the factorization quality and from EPS-side settings instead. The `ksp_rtol`, `ksp_atol`, and `ksp_max_it` knobs matter only on iterative paths, which is a common source of confusion worth stating twice.


## PC: preconditioners, LU, and MUMPS

**`PC`** (preconditioner) is the other half of the `KSP` split. A preconditioner approximates $A^{-1}$ cheaply so the outer iteration converges fast, or in our default case *is* $A^{-1}$ computed exactly by factorization.

**[`PCLU`](https://petsc.org/release/manualpages/PC/PCLU/)** means the preconditioner is an LU factorization: on setup it factors $A = LU$ (with pivoting), on apply it runs triangular solves. With `KSPPREONLY` in front, setup plus one apply equals a direct solve. In parallel the factorization itself is distributed (see MUMPS below).

**[`PCFactorSetMatSolverType`](https://petsc.org/release/manualpages/Mat/MATSOLVERMUMPS/)** selects *which* sparse direct package performs the LU inside `PCLU`. This one call is our entire backend seam. Resolution order in this repo: YAML `factor_backend`, then per-solver env override, then `LINSTABPY_FACTOR_BACKEND`, then the call-site default. An unavailable backend fails loudly during setup. It never falls back silently.

**[`MATSOLVERMUMPS`](https://petsc.org/release/manualpages/Mat/MATSOLVERMUMPS/) ([MUMPS](https://mumps-solver.org/))** is the default backend: a [MUltifrontal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multifrontal_method) Massively Parallel sparse direct Solver that factors distributed matrices across MPI ranks. "Multifrontal" names the algorithm family (dense frontal matrices eliminated in a tree order). Practical knobs exposed here: ordering selection mapped to MUMPS `ICNTL(7)` (`amd`, `pord`, `metis`, `qamd`, `auto`), optional block low-rank compression (`LINSTABPY_MUMPS_BLR` with tolerance), and precision selection. MUMPS uses dynamic pivoting, which is why the temporal eigensolver retries a failed STRUMPACK factor (static pivoting, `ZERO_PIVOT`) once with MUMPS.

**Other backends, one line each.** STRUMPACK: structured and rank-compressed direct and approximate solver, experimental here, used through FGMRES. [SuperLU_DIST](https://portal.nersc.gov/project/sparse/superlu/): distributed-memory sparse LU, experimental here, GPU offload unvalidated. cuDSS: NVIDIA GPU sparse direct LU, validated here *as a preconditioner inside FGMRES* (one rank, one GPU, with a second factorization of the conjugate transpose for [adjoint](https://grokipedia.com/page/Adjoint) applies), matching MUMPS to 1e-12 on tested cases, not as a PETSc-native factor type. The backend audit is the [compute backends](development/compute-backends.md) page.

**[`PCBJACOBI`](https://petsc.org/release/manualpages/PC/PCBJACOBI/) and [`PCASM`](https://petsc.org/release/manualpages/PC/PCASM/)** are [domain-decomposition](https://grokipedia.com/page/Domain_decomposition_methods) preconditioners: block Jacobi (each rank factors its own diagonal block, no overlap) and additive Schwarz (overlapping blocks). They appear as the baseline direction for the memory-bound iterative eigensolver path. One API trap the code documents: sub-preconditioner options must be applied *after* `EPS.setUp()`, or they attach to nothing.

**Transpose solves.** Adjoint work and $H^H$ applies need $A^H x = b$, not $Ax = b$. The factorization object exposes `solve_adjoint` alongside `solve`, reusing the same LU factors. No second factorization is needed for the adjoint half of resolvent or stability analysis.


## MatShell: matrices you never assemble

**[`MatCreateShell`](https://petsc.org/release/manualpages/Mat/MatCreateShell/)** creates a PETSc `Mat` with no stored entries. You register callback functions (at minimum the multiply `y = Ax`, optionally transpose and others) and PETSc treats the result as a matrix: it can sit inside `KSP`, `EPS`, and `ST` exactly like an assembled `AIJ` matrix. "Shell" contrasts with "assembled." The multiply runs your code, typically a few operator applies and triangular solves.

**Why the resolvent needs it.** The resolvent $H = C F ((\gamma - i\omega) I - L_0)^{-1} F B$ is dense even though $L_0$ is sparse. Forming it explicitly at $150{,}000$ unknowns is out of the question. Instead `WeightedNormalOperator` is a shell whose multiply chains existing cheap pieces: apply $H$ (two filters plus one factored solve plus $B$ and $C$ maps), weight by $W$, apply $H^H$ (adjoint filters plus one transpose solve), and for the [Chu](core-concepts.md) forcing norm multiply by $W^{-1}$. SLEPc then runs an eigensolver that only ever calls this multiply. [Gains](core-concepts.md) come out as $\sigma = \sqrt{\mathrm{Re}(\lambda)}$ without $H$ ever existing as entries.

**Ownership detail.** On multi-rank communicators the multiply callback writes only its rank's local row range into the result vector. Getting this wrong silently corrupts outer iterations, which is why the shell code is explicit about ranges.


## SLEPc: EPS eigensolvers and ST spectral transformations

**SLEPc** extends PETSc to eigenvalue problems. It operates on PETSc `Mat` and `Vec` objects, so everything in sections 2 to 5 carries over. Its Python binding is [slepc4py](https://slepc4py.readthedocs.io/en/stable/).

**[`EPS`](https://slepc.upv.es/documentation/current/docs/manualpages/EPS/EPSSetProblemType/)** (Eigenvalue Problem Solver) is the eigensolver object, the analogue of `KSP` for $Ax = \lambda Bx$. You set the problem type, the method, how many pairs you want, which ones, the tolerance, and the spectral transformation, then call solve and extract pairs one by one.

**Problem types ([`EPSSetProblemType`](https://slepc.upv.es/documentation/current/docs/manualpages/EPS/EPSSetProblemType/)).** This repo uses two. `NHEP`: standard ($B = I$) non-Hermitian problem, used for temporal stability ($\omega = \mathrm{eig}(iL_0)$) and for the weighted normal resolvent problem. `GNHEP`: generalized non-Hermitian $Ax = \lambda Bx$, used for spatial stability where the $B$ matrix carries boundary rows and algebraic constraints (and is often singular, which matters below). Hermitian types exist and are not used here because LNSE operators are [nonnormal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Defective_matrix).

**[`EPSKRYLOVSCHUR`](https://slepc.upv.es/documentation/current/docs/manualpages/EPS/EPSKRYLOVSCHUR/)** is the restarted Krylov-Schur eigensolver, our method on every path. Think restarted [Arnoldi](https://grokipedia.com/page/Arnoldi_iteration) with a cleaner restart: build a Krylov subspace, project the problem, keep the wanted Ritz information in a Krylov-Schur decomposition, expand again. After $m$ Arnoldi steps the factorization reads $AV = VH + \beta v_{m+1} e_m^T$ with $V$ orthonormal and $H$ upper Hessenberg. Each eigenpair $(\lambda_i, y_i)$ of the small $H$ lifts to a **Ritz pair** $(\lambda_i, Vy_i)$ of $A$, with residual exactly $|\beta|\,|e_m^T y_i|$, so convergence is tested with no extra matvecs. Krylov-Schur (Stewart, 2001) keeps $H$ in Schur form instead, which makes restarting clean: truncate to the wanted Schur vectors and expand again, bounding memory at subspace size rather than iteration count. Like all Krylov eigensolvers it finds exterior eigenvalues of the operator it sees, which is exactly why shift-invert (next object) precedes it for interior targets. Full development in Frantz, Loiseau and Robinet (2023), *Krylov methods for large-scale dynamical systems*, sections on Krylov subspaces and large-scale eigensolvers.

**[`EPSSetDimensions`](https://slepc.upv.es/documentation/current/docs/manualpages/EPS/EPSSetDimensions/)** sets `nev` (eigenpairs wanted) and `ncv` (Krylov subspace size, the accuracy and cost knob). `ncv` must exceed `nev`, and larger `ncv` helps crowded or nonnormal neighborhoods where small subspaces stall. Repo defaults: temporal uses $\max(2\cdot\mathrm{nev}+3, 30)$ clipped to matrix size; spatial uses $\min(\max(4\cdot\mathrm{nev}, 30), \mathrm{ndof}-1)$; resolvent uses $\min(\max(2\cdot\mathrm{nev}+3, 20), \mathrm{ndof}-1)$. A user-passed `ncv` must be larger than `nev` or setup raises.

**[`EPSSetWhichEigenpairs`](https://slepc.upv.es/documentation/current/docs/manualpages/EPS/EPSSetWhichEigenpairs/)** picks *which* eigenvalues to want. Temporal and spatial paths use `TARGET_MAGNITUDE`: closest to the shift target in magnitude, combined with shift-invert. The resolvent path uses `LARGEST_MAGNITUDE`: the normal operator's largest eigenvalues are the squared leading gains by construction, so no shift is needed there.

**Krylov convergence practice.** Two results from the review govern expectations. First, isolated eigenvalues converge geometrically fast while branches crawl: the error bound scales with $\kappa(V)\,(\rho/|\mu_i - c|)^k$ for an eigenvalue $\mu_i$ outside a disk of radius $\rho$, and dense branches are the worst case on both factors (poor isolation times large eigenvector conditioning from nonnormality). Crowded or branch-heavy targets are exactly where raising `ncv` pays. Second, Arnoldi favors eigenvectors with large components in the starting vector, so genuinely random starts are the default unless prior knowledge says otherwise; a start nearly orthogonal to the wanted mode stalls. Time-stepper codes add heuristics this repo does not need (matrix-forming factors replace sampling periods), but the diagnosis transfers: slow convergence near a branch means widen the subspace or move the shift, not just tighten the tolerance. See Frantz, Loiseau and Robinet (2023), observations on eigenvalue convergence.

**[`EPSSetTolerances`](https://slepc.upv.es/documentation/current/docs/manualpages/EPS/EPSSetTolerances/)** sets the eigenpair tolerance and restart limit. Three finer points the code exposes: the *convergence test* (`abs`, `rel`, or `norm`) decides how the residual is measured during the solve; the *reported residual* need not equal the tested one; and `true_residual=true` forces the expensive untransformed residual on shift-invert runs, because the cheap transformed estimate can look converged while the true pair is poor. Temporal and resolvent tolerances come from YAML (`eps_tol`, `eps_max_it`); spatial currently uses fixed `tol=1e-10`, `max_it=max(500, 10\cdot\mathrm{ndof})`. Monitor output (`-eps_monitor`) prints per-restart convergence and is the first thing to ask for when a spectrum looks wrong.

**[`ST`](https://slepc.upv.es/documentation/current/docs/manualpages/ST/STSetShift/) and [`STSINVERT`](https://slepc.upv.es/documentation/current/docs/manualpages/ST/STSINVERT/)** (spectral transformation, shift-invert). Krylov methods find exterior eigenvalues, but stability targets sit in the spectrum interior. Shift-invert replaces the operator with $(A - \sigma B)^{-1} B$, whose *largest* eigenvalues are exactly the $\lambda$ closest to the shift $\sigma$, with eigenvectors unchanged. Each `ST` apply is one linear solve with the shifted matrix, which is why the `KSPPREONLY` + `PCLU` + MUMPS factor from sections 3 and 4 sits underneath every shift-invert eigensolve. [`STSetShift`](https://slepc.upv.es/documentation/current/docs/manualpages/ST/STSetShift/) sets $\sigma$. This repo sets the shift explicitly on `ST` rather than relying only on `EPS.setTarget`, so the generalized shift center is never implicit. Temporal targets live in $\omega$ space ($\sigma$ near the wanted $\omega$); the solver internally handles the $iL_0$ scaling.


## The exact chains this repo runs

One scoping note: this repo is matrix-forming (assembled $L_0$ plus direct factors), not matrix-free time-stepping, so the review's Newton-Krylov, monodromy, and sampling-period machinery does not apply here. What transfers fully is the Krylov eigensolver core below: Arnoldi factorization, Ritz convergence, and shift-invert.

| Analysis | Operator seen by EPS | EPS setup | ST and linear backend |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Temporal EVP** | $iL_0$, target $\sigma$ in $\omega$ space | `NHEP`, Krylov-Schur, `TARGET_MAGNITUDE`, YAML tol and max it | `SINVERT` at $\sigma$, factorize-once `KSPPREONLY` + `PCLU` + MUMPS |
| **Spatial EVP** | $(A, R)$ block pair | `GNHEP`, Krylov-Schur, `TARGET_MAGNITUDE`, `tol=1e-10` | `SINVERT`, same direct backend. Tiny or near-full problems (`ndof ≤ 2` or `nev ≥ ndof-1`) switch to dense QZ (`scipy.linalg.eig`) because $R$ is singular from BC rows and QZ handles that natively. |
| **Resolvent gain** | Shell: $W^{-1}H^HWH$ (`chu`) or $H^HWH$ (`l2`) | `NHEP`, Krylov-Schur, `LARGEST_MAGNITUDE`, YAML tol and max it | No `ST`. Each shell multiply applies $H$ and $H^H$ through one `KSPPREONLY` + `PCLU` factor of $L_\sigma$. |
| **Router reuse** | Nearby $K(\omega)$ | Same gain EPS per point | Anchor factor as *right preconditioner* inside GMRES (restart 50, max 200). Residual gate decides reuse, refactor, or defer. |
| **Adjoint EVP** | $W^{-1}L_0^H W$ (SciPy path) | Same temporal EPS shape near mapped target | Transpose solves through the existing factors. |
| **Iterative opt-ins** | Same operators | Same EPS shape | `fgmres_lu` or `strumpack_fgmres`, explicit policy only, with `true_residual` defaulted on because transformed residuals can lie. |

Two boundaries worth memorizing. A direct factor belongs to exactly one shift $(\omega, \gamma)$. Reuse across shifts happens only as router preconditioning under a residual gate, never as an exact solve. And iterative linear solvers are never automatic downgrade from direct factors. They require explicit solver policy so accuracy changes stay visible.


## Knobs: YAML, env, and options database

| Knob | Where | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `solver.eigen` / `solver.spatial` / `solver.resolvent` YAML blocks | Case file | Targets, `nev`, `ncv`, `eps_tol`, `eps_max_it`, convergence test, true residual flag, monitor flag per analysis. Spatial falls back to the eigen block when absent. |
| `factor_backend` | YAML solver subsection, then `LINSTABPY_FACTOR_BACKEND`, then call-site default | Which package backs `PCLU`: `mumps` (default), `strumpack`, `superlu_dist`, `cudss` route. Per-solver env overrides exist for eigen and resolvent paths. |
| `LINSTABPY_MUMPS_ORDERING`, `LINSTABPY_MUMPS_BLR`, `LINSTABPY_MUMPS_BLR_TOL`, `LINSTABPY_FACTOR_PRECISION` | Env | MUMPS ordering, low-rank compression, factor precision on paths that consume them. |
| `ncv`, `eps_tol`, `eps_max_it`, `conv_test`, `true_residual`, `monitor` | YAML `eps` subsection | Subspace size, tolerance, restart cap, how convergence is measured, whether to compute true residuals, whether to print monitor lines. |
| `-eps_monitor`, `-ksp_monitor`, `-eps_view`, … | Options database (after `--`) | Runtime inspection without editing files. `-eps_monitor` is the single most useful flag when a spectrum misbehaves. |
| `ksp_rtol`, `ksp_atol`, `ksp_max_it`, `pc_type` | YAML, iterative paths only | Meaningful only when a real Krylov iteration runs. Inert on `KSPPREONLY`. |


## Choosing a configuration

Start here when the knobs in [Knobs](#knobs-yaml-env-and-options-database) feel like too many degrees of freedom. Every number below is measured on the Savarino resolvent case (450k unknowns, 23.4M nonzeros, dual Xeon Silver 4210R) unless stated otherwise.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Q1{"Does a direct factor fit in memory?"}
    Q1 -->|Yes| D1["Direct: KSPPREONLY + PCLU + MUMPS"]
    Q1 -->|No| I1["Iterative, explicit opt-in: fgmres_lu or strumpack_fgmres with true_residual on"]
    D1 --> Q2{"One point or a map?"}
    Q2 -->|One point| P1["Single factorize, single EPS. Done."]
    Q2 -->|Map over frequencies| Q3{"Lines or farm?"}
    Q3 -->|Few points, many nodes| F1["Farm: independent jobs per point (83.6 min for 200 points, 5 concurrent)"]
    Q3 -->|Dense lines| L1["Line driver: assemble once, anchor factors, in-place numeric refactorization (59.7 min for the same 200)"]
    D1 --> Q4{"Which mesh?"}
    Q4 -->|Rectilinear, leak at round-off| E0["epsilon = 0. Check insensitivity under refinement."]
    Q4 -->|Bent, leak order one| E1["Dissipation on. Tune epsilon on this mesh until the gain or eigenvalue stops moving."]
```

Why the defaults are the defaults, with the measurements behind them:

| Decision | Evidence |
|---|---|
| Direct first | One point costs 60 s factorize from scratch (54 s numeric refactor reusing symbolic analysis), 0.44 s per forward solve, 0.43 s per adjoint solve, 5.8 s for the gain eigensolve. The factor is four fifths of a point; everything else is noise next to it. |
| Small Krylov spaces | Cutting `ncv` from 20 to 5 cut solves per point from 40 to 10 and moved the gain by less than $10^{-10}$. Subspace size sets cost, not precision, past the threshold. |
| Trust but verify reuse | Farm and line modes agree on all 200 map gains to $4.7\times 10^{-10}$ relative (median $7.9\times 10^{-11}$). Worst residuals over the map: $8.0\times 10^{-8}$ forward, $9.8\times 10^{-9}$ adjoint. Reuse without residuals is hope; with residuals it is a method. |
| Dissipation by measurement | Leak below $10^{-11}$ (Song, Savarino meshes): $\varepsilon = 0$ is the declared choice, moving gains by at most 1.4% when raised to 0.1. Leak order one (bent meshes): dissipation required. Full procedure in the [FAQ](faq.md). |
| Ranks last | 4 to 16 ranks bought 22% less time for twice the memory (18.6 to 40.6 GiB) on one point. Scale out across cases before scaling up ranks. |

All figures: the linstabpy paper, computational performance section, with per-point CSVs under `examples/savarino/`.

## Reading list

In the order I would read them:

1. Frantz, Loiseau and Robinet (2023), *Krylov methods for large-scale dynamical systems: application in fluid dynamics*, *Appl. Mech. Rev.* 75(3), 030802. The review behind sections 3, 5, and 6 of this page: Arnoldi factorization, Ritz convergence, non-modal bounds, and Krylov practice in fluids.
2. The [PETSc KSP manual chapter](https://petsc.org/release/manual/ksp/). Linear solves, `KSP` with `PC`, direct versus iterative, the options database. Covers sections 2 to 4 of this page with examples.
3. [`KSPPREONLY`](https://petsc.org/release/manualpages/KSP/KSPPREONLY/) and [`PCLU`](https://petsc.org/release/manualpages/PC/PCLU/). Short pages. Together they are our default solve.
4. [`MATSOLVERMUMPS`](https://petsc.org/release/manualpages/Mat/MATSOLVERMUMPS/) and the [MUMPS homepage](https://mumps-solver.org/). What the default factor backend does and its controls.
5. [`MatCreateShell`](https://petsc.org/release/manualpages/Mat/MatCreateShell/). Matrix-free operators in PETSc vocabulary.
6. [`EPSSetProblemType`](https://slepc.upv.es/documentation/current/docs/manualpages/EPS/EPSSetProblemType/), [`EPSKRYLOVSCHUR`](https://slepc.upv.es/documentation/current/docs/manualpages/EPS/EPSKRYLOVSCHUR/), [`STSINVERT`](https://slepc.upv.es/documentation/current/docs/manualpages/ST/STSINVERT/). The three pages behind every eigensolve here.
7. [petsc4py](https://petsc4py.readthedocs.io/en/stable/) and [slepc4py](https://slepc4py.readthedocs.io/en/stable/) docs. Python-side API used throughout `src/`.
8. [SciPy sparse matrices](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/sparse.html). CSC and CSR formats behind the assembly side of the dual path.
9. Schmid and Henningson, *Stability and [Transition](http://www.scholarpedia.org/article/Transition_to_turbulence) in Shear Flows* (Springer, 2001). The fluids-side companion: what the eigenvalues and gains mean physically once the solvers return them.

If a solver term appears elsewhere in this wiki without a link, that is a bug in that page. Link it here.

# References

The papers and manuals behind this wiki, grouped by what they justify. One line each on why it is cited. To cite this software, see [how to cite](index.md#cite-linstabpy) on the home page.

## The package and its lineage

* Hamada, G. Y. R., Wolf, W. R., Junqueira-Junior, C., Robinet, J.-C. and Frantz, R. A. S. LinStabPy: an efficient Python framework for compressible stability and resolvent analysis. *Theor. Comput. Fluid Dyn.* (under revision, 2026). The paper for this codebase. Prefer it when citing results.
* Martini, E. and Schmidt, O. T. (2024). LinStab2D: stability and resolvent analysis of compressible viscous flows in MATLAB. *Theor. Comput. Fluid Dyn.* 38, 665–685. doi:10.1007/s00162-024-00706-0. The methodology ancestor: linearized equations, SBP discretization, metrics, boundary conditions, filtering. Cite alongside the linstabpy paper.
* Padovan, A., Anantharaman, V., Rowley, C. W., Vollmer, B., Colonius, T. and Bodony, D. J. (2025). resolvent4py: a parallel Python package for analysis, model reduction and control of large-scale linear systems. *SoftwareX* 31, 102286. doi:10.1016/j.softx.2025.102286. Operator-handling design influence.

## Stability and transition theory

* Schmid, P. J. and Henningson, D. S. (2001). *Stability and Transition in Shear Flows*. Springer. The textbook companion for modal spectra, branches, and transition physics.
* Schmid, P. J. (2007). Nonmodal stability theory. *Annu. Rev. Fluid Mech.* 39, 129–162. Transient growth, optimal perturbations, and the finite-time viewpoint behind gain maps.
* Trefethen, L. N., Trefethen, A. E., Reddy, S. C. and Driscoll, T. A. (1993). Hydrodynamic stability without eigenvalues. *Science* 261, 578–584. Why spectra alone mislead for nonnormal operators; the founding case for pseudospectra thinking.
* Frantz, R. A. S., Loiseau, J.-Ch. and Robinet, J.-Ch. (2023). Krylov methods for large-scale dynamical systems: application in fluid dynamics. *Appl. Mech. Rev.* 75(3), 030802. doi:10.1115/1.4056808. Arnoldi factorization, Ritz convergence, modal vs non-modal bounds, Krylov practice. The review behind the [solver glossary](solver-glossary.md).
* Hanifi, A., Schmid, P. J. and Henningson, D. S. (1996). Transient growth in compressible boundary layer flow. *Phys. Fluids* 8, 826–837. doi:10.1063/1.868864. Compressible transient growth; the wall-normal mapping parameter in the Blasius example follows this work.

## Resolvent and adjoint methods

* McKeon, B. J. and Sharma, A. S. (2010). A critical-layer framework for turbulent pipe flow. *J. Fluid Mech.* 658, 336–382. Resolvent framing for amplifier flows.
* Luchini, P. and Bottaro, A. (2014). Adjoint equations in stability analysis. *Annu. Rev. Fluid Mech.* 46, 493–. The adjoint machinery behind receptivity and wavemaker fields.
* Chu, B.-T. (1965). On the energy transfer to small disturbances in fluid flow (Part I). *Acta Mech.* 1(3), 215–234. The compressible energy inner product used for every gain and norm here.

## Discretization

* Strand, B. (1994). Summation by parts for finite difference approximations for d/dx. *J. Comput. Phys.* 110(1), 47–67. First-derivative SBP operators.
* Mattsson, K. and Nordstrom, J. (2004). Summation by parts operators for finite difference approximations of second derivatives. *J. Comput. Phys.* 199(2), 503–540. Second-derivative SBP operators.
* Mattsson, K., Svard, M. and Nordstrom, J. (2004). Stable and accurate artificial dissipation. *J. Sci. Comput.* 21, 57–79. doi:10.1023/B:JOMP.0000027955.75872.3f. The dissipation operator behind the epsilon knob.
* Linders, V., Lundquist, T. and Nordstrom, J. (2018). On the order of accuracy of finite difference operators on diagonal norm based summation-by-parts form. *SIAM J. Numer. Anal.* 56, 1048–1063. doi:10.1137/17M1139333. Why diagonal-norm boundary closures lose order — and why only even orders 2, 4, 6, 8 ship here.
* Lele, S. K. (1992). Compact finite difference schemes with spectral-like resolution. *J. Comput. Phys.* 103, 16–42. Centered stencils annihilate the sawtooth mode at any order; the reason grid-scale content needs watching.
* Fornberg, B. (1988). Generation of finite difference formulas on arbitrarily spaced grids. *Math. Comp.* 51, 699–706. Weight generation behind the mesh operators.

## Solver stack

* Balay, S. et al. (2025). *PETSc/TAO Users Manual* (ANL-21/39, Rev. 3.24). Argonne National Laboratory. doi:10.2172/2998643. Distributed matrices, KSP/PC, the runtime under every solve.
* Hernandez, V., Roman, J. E. and Vidal, V. (2005). SLEPc: a scalable and flexible toolkit for the solution of eigenvalue problems. *ACM Trans. Math. Software* 31(3), 351–362. doi:10.1145/1089014.1089019. EPS eigensolvers and spectral transformations.
* Amestoy, P. R., Duff, I. S., Koster, J. and L'Excellent, J.-Y. (2001). A fully asynchronous multifrontal solver using distributed dynamic scheduling. *SIAM J. Matrix Anal. Appl.* 23(1), 15–41. MUMPS, the default sparse-direct backend.

## Installation

Source: https://linstabpy.vercel.app/installation/

# Installation

One supported numerical stack: **CPU, complex-scalar PETSc/SLEPc, MUMPS**.
That is the merge-gate and example path. Two ways to build it: `install.sh`
or `environment.yml`. GPU is not an install path yet.

| Path | Prefix | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `install.sh` | `.venv` | Reference workstation build. Default PETSc 3.24 with MUMPS. |
| `environment.yml` | conda env `linstabpy` | Same contract from conda-forge. pip installs this package only. |
| GPU / `environment-gpu.yml` | — | Not shipped. See [GPU and extra stacks](#gpu-and-extra-stacks). |

The [compute backends](development/compute-backends.md) page is the backend audit. This section is how you install.

## Prerequisites

Use the repository scripts first. They check compilers, [MPI](https://grokipedia.com/page/Message_Passing_Interface), Python bindings,
PETSc/SLEPc, and the runtime stack that the examples will use.

Required system tools:

- POSIX shell with `bash`
- C, C++, and Fortran compilers
- `make`, `cmake`, `curl`, and `pkg-config`
- one MPI stack with development headers (`mpicc`, `mpicxx`, `mpifort`, `mpiexec`)
- a Python environment managed by the repository installer
- HDF5 development files (optional, only for MATLAB v7.3 / HDF5 tooling)

Do not mix MPI stacks in one environment. PETSc, SLEPc, `mpi4py`, and the runtime
`mpiexec` must agree on the same MPI ABI.

## Linux (recommended): `install.sh`

Clone the repository and run the native checks:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/openfluids/linstabpy.git
cd linstabpy

bash install.sh --diagnose
bash install.sh
bash install.sh --check
bash examples/benchmark.sh
```

The reference MATLAB base flows (`M09jet.mat`, `BL_BF.mat`, `Step_BF.mat`,
`Paraboloid_BF.mat`) used by the Martini example loaders ship in
`examples/linstab2d/baseflows/`. See
[Reference base flows](https://github.com/openfluids/linstabpy#reference-base-flows)
for the data of the other examples.

`install.sh --diagnose` is read-only. It checks compilers, MPI launchers, development
headers, dual-MPI conflicts, and whether `mpiexec -n 1 /bin/true` works.

`install.sh` creates `.venv`, builds or installs the Python/PETSc/SLEPc stack,
repairs `mpi4py` when the wheel ABI does not match the selected MPI stack, and
installs this repository in editable mode.

Use `--force` for a clean reinstall. It removes the existing `.venv` first, then
rebuilds the full Python, PETSc/SLEPc, `mpi4py`, `petsc4py`, and `slepc4py`
environment:

```bash
bash install.sh --force
```

Use `--latest` only when you deliberately want the newest compatible package
releases instead of the pinned PETSc/SLEPc family used by the default installer:

```bash
bash install.sh --force --latest
```

`install.sh` uses the Python version in `.python-version` (3.14), the same
version CI tests. To build with another version, set it explicitly:

```bash
LINSTABPY_PYTHON_VERSION=3.13 bash install.sh --force
```

For reproducible comparisons, record the Python version printed by
`install.sh --check`.

`install.sh --check` verifies that `petsc4py` and `slepc4py` import, that PETSc
uses complex scalars, and that a small SLEPc non-Hermitian Krylov-Schur solve
works from Python.

`examples/benchmark.sh` runs a small benchmark and writes benchmark artifacts under
`benchmark_runs/<run-id>/`.

By default, the installer does not call `sudo` or a package manager. If required
system tools are missing, it prints the commands and stops. On a normal
workstation, opt in to package-manager installation explicitly:

```bash
LINSTABPY_AUTO_INSTALL_SYS_DEPS=1 bash install.sh
```

On a provisioned workstation or cluster node, skip the system dependency check:

```bash
LINSTABPY_SKIP_SYS_DEPS=1 bash install.sh
```

## Conda: `environment.yml` (CPU)

This file is the CPU path for people who already use conda. conda-forge supplies
Python, NumPy/SciPy, and a **complex-scalar** PETSc/SLEPc/`mpi4py` stack.
pip then installs `linstabpy` from PyPI with `--no-deps`, so pip does not pull a
second NumPy or compile PETSc. No checkout is needed:
`conda env create -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/openfluids/linstabpy/main/environment.yml`.

Python is `>=3.11,<3.15`. The installer default is 3.14, and conda-forge
resolves 3.14 with complex PETSc 3.24.

```bash
# Unset PETSC_DIR, PETSC_ARCH, and SLEPC_DIR first.
# A leftover PETSc prefix will bind petsc4py to the wrong build.
conda env create -f environment.yml
conda activate linstabpy
python -c "import numpy as np; from petsc4py import PETSc; assert np.issubdtype(PETSc.ScalarType, np.complexfloating)"
```

Do not add `petsc4py`, `slepc4py`, or `mpi4py` to the pip list. Those source
packages compile PETSc and fight the conda MPI stack. The reference route is
`bash install.sh`.

`environment.yml` is not a second reference build. If conda-forge PETSc is a
different minor than `install.sh` (3.24 + MUMPS), record both versions. A
failing SLEPc NHEP probe or a real-scalar PETSc means the env is unusable for
this code, even if `import linstabpy` works.

## GPU and extra stacks

Do not add `environment-gpu.yml` or a second named conda env. CPU and GPU PETSc
cannot share one prefix, so two isolated installs will be the right shape
**after** a GPU stack has a green `install.sh --check` and a passing
EVP/resolvent residual. That has not happened.

| Stack | How it exists today |
|---|---|
| CPU, complex PETSc, MUMPS | Live. `.venv` via `install.sh`, or conda env `linstabpy`. |
| `gpu-strumpack` | Design only. `bash install.sh --stack gpu-strumpack --dry-run` prints the plan. `--force` may only touch `.venv-gpu-strumpack`, never `.venv`. No GPU build is claimed. |
| SuperLU_DIST + CUDA, complex | Tested on one CUDA build; solve residuals were order one. Rejected for that path. |

`LINSTABPY_FACTOR_BACKEND=strumpack` is an experimental **CPU** factor choice
when that library is in the PETSc build. It is not a GPU install. See the
[compute backends](development/compute-backends.md) page.

## macOS

macOS uses the same `install.sh --diagnose` → `install.sh` → `install.sh --check` →
`examples/benchmark.sh` flow as Linux. The only difference is the [BLAS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BLAS)/ScaLAPACK setup
below.

For the macOS PETSc/SLEPc path, install Homebrew OpenBLAS and ScaLAPACK before
building when possible:

```bash
brew install openblas scalapack
```

The reason is a macOS runtime-library ordering issue in Python. PETSc's
downloaded ScaLAPACK can resolve [LAPACK](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LAPACK) symbols to Apple Accelerate when loaded
inside Python. The failing path observed in this repository was Python
`slepc4py` `EPS_NHEP` with Krylov-Schur / [Arnoldi](https://grokipedia.com/page/Arnoldi_iteration), aborting inside Accelerate
`ZLADIV`. Native C SLEPc NHEP worked, and Python HEP/LAPACK paths worked, which
pointed to dynamic-library symbol interposition rather than the examples.

The current installer handles this by preferring Homebrew OpenBLAS/ScaLAPACK at
PETSc configure time and by wrapping `.venv/bin/python` so Homebrew OpenBLAS is
loaded before Python imports NumPy, PETSc, or SLEPc. `install.sh --check` runs a
tiny Python `EPS_NHEP` Krylov-Schur probe, so this crash is detected before
examples are run.

On macOS, do not use `uv run` to run LinStabPy examples after installation. It
can bypass the patched `.venv` and try to rebuild `petsc4py`/`slepc4py` from
source with the wrong runtime layout. Use `.venv/bin/python` directly:

```bash
.venv/bin/python -m examples.linstab2d.example_1_blasius
```

## Clusters and Intel MPI

On clusters, load the compiler/MPI modules before running the installer. The
repository scripts should see the same `mpicc`, `mpicxx`, `mpifort`, and
`mpiexec` that will be used at runtime.

Generic module workflow:

```bash
module load <compiler-module> <mpi-module>
bash install.sh --diagnose
bash install.sh
bash install.sh --check
```

Intel MPI / oneAPI workflow:

```bash
source /opt/intel/oneapi/setvars.sh --force
export LINSTABPY_MPI_STACK=intelmpi
export I_MPI_CC=gcc
export I_MPI_CXX=g++
export I_MPI_F90=gfortran
export I_MPI_FC=gfortran

bash install.sh --diagnose
bash install.sh
bash install.sh --check
```

Use Intel MPI only when `install.sh --diagnose` shows that the active MPI compiler wrappers
and `mpiexec` come from the Intel MPI environment and the MPI compile probe
passes. Do not use an Intel MPI launcher with Open MPI or MPICH Python bindings.

## Environment variables

| Variable | Default | Use |
|---|---:|---|
| `LINSTABPY_WITH_H5PY` | `0` | Set to `1` to install `h5py` for MATLAB v7.3 / HDF5 parity tooling. Leave unset for the normal solver install. |
| `LINSTABPY_MPI_STACK` | auto | Set to `intelmpi` when an Intel MPI environment is already loaded and should be used. Otherwise the scripts infer the active stack. |
| `LINSTABPY_AUTO_INSTALL_SYS_DEPS` | `0` | Set to `1` to allow `install.sh` to call the system package manager for missing Linux dependencies. |
| `LINSTABPY_PETSC_MPIEXEC` | auto | Path to the `mpiexec` PETSc/SLEPc configure should use. Set this when the default launcher hangs or is not the runtime launcher you want. |
| `LINSTABPY_MPI4PY_NO_BINARY` | `0` | Set to `1` to force `mpi4py` to build from source against the active MPI stack. |
| `LINSTABPY_VERIFY_MPIEXEC` | auto | Path to the `mpiexec` used by `install.sh --check` for MPI import/probe checks. |
| `LINSTABPY_SKIP_SYS_DEPS` | `0` | Set to `1` to skip Linux system dependency detection and package-manager advice. |

## Activation and shell aliases

You can run everything through `.venv/bin/python` without activating the
environment:

```bash
.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/
```

For interactive work, activation is still convenient:

```bash
source .venv/bin/activate
```

If you use the project often, add a small alias or shell function to your
`~/.bashrc` / `~/.zshrc` so you do not have to remember the activation path:

```bash
alias linstabpy-activate='cd /path/to/linstabpy && source .venv/bin/activate'
```

Keep the path local to your machine. The alias is optional and should not be used
in scripts; scripts should call `.venv/bin/python` directly so logs show which
interpreter ran.

## MPI stack verification

The installer chooses one active MPI stack from the shell environment. The same
stack must own all of these pieces:

- `mpicc`, `mpicxx`, and `mpifort`
- the `mpiexec` used by PETSc/SLEPc configure
- `mpi4py`
- `petsc4py` and `slepc4py`
- the `mpiexec` used for runtime examples and tests

Read the install log rather than guessing. A healthy install prints the MPI
launcher used for PETSc/SLEPc configure, the launcher used for verification, the
resolved MPI library directory, and the result of single-rank and multi-rank
checks. If those paths point to different MPI families, rebuild from a clean
environment:

```bash
rm -rf .venv
bash install.sh --diagnose
bash install.sh --force
bash install.sh --check
```

For clusters with Intel MPI, source oneAPI or the site module first and make that
choice explicit:

```bash
source /opt/intel/oneapi/setvars.sh --force
export LINSTABPY_MPI_STACK=intelmpi
bash install.sh --diagnose
bash install.sh --force
bash install.sh --check
```

Do not repair a mixed MPI install by editing `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` until it happens
to import. Reinstall with the intended MPI stack visible from the start.

## Known-good reference stacks

A healthy Linux install should satisfy this sequence:

```bash
bash install.sh --diagnose
bash install.sh --check
bash examples/run_all_examples.sh --mpi -n 1 -m examples.linstab2d.example_1_blasius
bash examples/benchmark.sh
```

One known-good Linux profile used during hardening was:

| Component | Reference value |
|---|---|
| OS family | Ubuntu 24.04 class |
| MPI | Open MPI 4.1.6 class |
| Python | 3.13 class |
| PETSc/SLEPc scalar type | complex |
| Sparse direct solver | MUMPS through PETSc |
| Thread policy | one BLAS/OpenMP thread per MPI rank |

Use this as a comparison shape, not a hard pin. A working install records the
Python version, PETSc/SLEPc versions, and scalar type in `install.sh --check`.

## MPI runtime rules

Use one MPI stack per install and one thread per rank unless you are measuring a
different layout on purpose.

For manual MPI runs:

```bash
export OMP_NUM_THREADS=1
export MKL_NUM_THREADS=1
export OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1
export NUMEXPR_NUM_THREADS=1
export VECLIB_MAXIMUM_THREADS=1
```

These defaults prevent every MPI rank from also starting a full BLAS/OpenMP
thread pool. They are the right starting point for sparse direct solves and
postcheck-heavy runs. Increase them only for a controlled benchmark, and record
the changed values with the run log because they affect wall time, memory
pressure, and reproducibility.

Prefer the canonical example runner for MPI examples:

```bash
bash examples/run_all_examples.sh --mpi -m examples.linstab2d.example_1_blasius
bash examples/run_all_examples.sh --mpi -n 10 -m examples.linstab2d.example_3_streaky_bl
bash examples/run_all_examples.sh --mpi -n 1 -m examples.linstab2d.example_1_blasius -- -eps_monitor
```

If `-n/--ranks` is omitted in `--mpi` mode, the runner starts from half of the
detected physical cores. Override the launcher with `LINSTABPY_MPIEXEC` and the
default rank count with `LINSTABPY_MPI_RANKS` when the target machine needs an
explicit MPI runtime. For sparse direct factorization, more ranks are not
automatically faster; compare rank counts on the target machine.

---

## Troubleshooting

Source: https://linstabpy.vercel.app/troubleshooting/

# Troubleshooting

## macOS SLEPc NHEP crash

Symptom:

- Python `slepc4py` `EPS_NHEP` with Krylov-Schur / Arnoldi aborts
- native C SLEPc NHEP works
- Python HEP and LAPACK-backed paths work

Root cause: Apple Accelerate LAPACK symbols can be interposed ahead of the LAPACK
symbols expected by PETSc-downloaded ScaLAPACK inside a Python process.

Fix:

- install Homebrew OpenBLAS and ScaLAPACK
- run `bash install.sh` so PETSc is configured with those libraries when possible
- use the `.venv/bin/python` wrapper generated by the installer

Detection:

```bash
bash install.sh --check
```

The check includes a tiny Python SLEPc `EPS_NHEP` Krylov-Schur solve.

## Linux MPI compile failure

If `install.sh --diagnose` reports an MPI compile failure with `mpi.h` missing, install the
development package for the MPI stack you intend to use. On Ubuntu with Open MPI,
the needed packages are:

```bash
sudo apt install -y libopenmpi-dev openmpi-bin
```

On clusters, load the complete MPI/compiler module instead of installing system
packages.

## Dual-MPI conflict

If Open MPI, MPICH, and/or Intel MPI are all visible, choose one stack, make it
first in `PATH`, and reinstall from a clean `.venv`. Do not let PETSc build against
one MPI while `mpiexec` launches another.

## `mpi4py` ABI mismatch

If `mpi4py` imports fail after switching MPI stacks:

```bash
rm -rf .venv
uv cache clean
LINSTABPY_MPI4PY_NO_BINARY=1 bash install.sh
```

## PETSc configure hang

If PETSc configure hangs or fails on the wrong launcher:

```bash
LINSTABPY_PETSC_MPIEXEC=/path/to/working/mpiexec bash install.sh
```

Use the same launcher for verification when needed:

```bash
LINSTABPY_VERIFY_MPIEXEC=/path/to/working/mpiexec bash install.sh --check
```

## Intel MPI

Load a complete Intel MPI / oneAPI environment before running
`install.sh --diagnose` or `install.sh`. Do not combine an Intel MPI `mpiexec`
with Open MPI or MPICH Python bindings.

```bash
source /opt/intel/oneapi/setvars.sh --force
export LINSTABPY_MPI_STACK=intelmpi
bash install.sh --diagnose
bash install.sh
```

## What to send when a machine is still broken

Send:

- full `install.sh --diagnose` output
- full `install.sh` output
- `benchmark_runs/<run-id>/benchmark_summary.csv`
- relevant `benchmark_runs/<run-id>/*.log`
- the versions printed by `install.sh --check`

Installer experiments belong in the private working notes, not in this tree.

---

## Development workflow

Source: https://linstabpy.vercel.app/development/development/

# Development and Release Workflow

linstabpy is developed in small, verified increments. The public target is
`1.0.0`: one field loader, one YAML shape, and no compatibility shims.

## Branches

| Branch | Role |
|---|---|
| `main` | The only long-lived branch. Always passes the full suite. Every release is tagged here. |
| Topic branches | `feat/*`, `fix/*`, `refactor/*`, `test/*`, `docs/*`. Short-lived; branch from `main`, PR back into `main`. |
| Feature branches `vX.Y-*` | A feature that needs more validation before a release (for example `v1.1-prescribed-forcing`). Kept rebased on `main`; merged when its release is cut. |

## Versioning

- **Patch `0.0.x` / `1.0.x`** — one small, verified increment.
- **Minor `x.y.0`** — a completed milestone.
- **Major `1.0.0`** — first committed-stable public API.

`pyproject.toml`'s `version` on `main` equals the latest tag, or the next
target with a `.devN` suffix between releases, so an install from an untagged
commit never claims to be a release.

## The micro-release loop

1. **Pick a slice** that forms one coherent piece of work.
2. **Implement** on a topic branch.
3. **Verify** — the merge gate below. Keep it green at every commit.
4. **Changelog** — add entries under `[Unreleased]` in `CHANGELOG.md` as the
   work lands.
5. **Merge** — when the slice is coherent and green, open a PR into `main`.
6. **Tag** — on merge, cut the next tag on `main`.

## Merge gate — what must hold before a PR into `main`

1. **Full suite green on a machine with PETSc/SLEPc** —
   `PYTHONPATH=src .venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/ -q`.
2. **PETSc-free lane green** — loader, YAML, I/O, schema, and operator
   tests that collect without `mpi4py`.
3. **Frozen-numerics intact** — the hash-frozen validated-math files
   (operator coefficients, energy norm, SBP operators/generator) are unchanged.
   Any genuine math change carries an independent `< 1e-10` oracle parity,
   and the freeze hash is never re-baselined to pass.
4. **Lint/format clean** — `ruff check .` and `ruff format --check .`.
5. **No stray changes** — only files that trace to the slice; named-file staging
   only (never `git add -A`).
6. **Changelog updated** — the slice's user-visible changes are recorded.

GitHub Actions runs the PETSc-free lane and the tracked-file-size check.
It does not compile PETSc. The full suite is the workstation merge gate.

## Where verification runs

The development machines are memory-limited; the full merge gate runs on a
big-memory verification workstation. The loop:

1. Commit on the development machine and push the topic branch.
2. On the verification workstation, check out that branch (`git fetch && git
   checkout <branch> && git pull --ff-only`) and run the full merge gate there
   — the suite, the PETSc-free lane, and lint.
3. Merge the PR into `main` only after the gate is green on the verification
   workstation. A state that is green only on a development laptop is never
   merged.

Never copy edited sources to the verification machine by hand (no rsync/scp):
it runs exactly what the branch has, so every result stays traceable to a
commit SHA.

## Releasing — cutting a tag on `main`

1. In `CHANGELOG.md`, move the `[Unreleased]` entries into a new dated section.
2. Set `pyproject.toml` `version` to that tag.
3. Merge the release PR into `main` through the gate.
4. Annotated tag: `git tag -a vX.Y.Z <commit> -m "…"` then
   `git push origin vX.Y.Z`. **Never move a published tag**.
5. On `main`, bump `pyproject.toml` to the next `.devN` and open a fresh
   `[Unreleased]` heading in the changelog.

## Documentation site

`docs/` holds everything the website needs: `mkdocs.yml`, `vercel.json`,
`pages/` (the Markdown pages), `overrides/` (theme templates) and `scripts/`
(the generators). It also holds the LaTeX tutorial (`tutorial/`) and the README
banners (`assets/`), which are not on the site.

The pages are hand-owned. An early version was machine-generated, then
rewritten by hand (prose, links, examples, nav), so edit pages directly.
This page, [compute backends](compute-backends.md), and the
[runtime NPZ contract](runtime-npz-contract.md) live in `docs/pages/development/`.
Two scripts generate parts of the site, and CI runs both (`.github/workflows/docs.yml`):

- `python3 docs/scripts/generate_wiki_boundaries.py` rewrites the generated regions
  of [boundaries](../boundaries.md) (CLI variables, allowed YAML keys, lazy exports).
  It leaves the rest of the page unchanged.
- `python3 docs/scripts/generate_llms_full.py` writes `docs/pages/llms-full.txt`. Do not
  edit that file by hand.

Add `--check` to either script to fail when its output is stale.

Build the site in its own environment. `uv run` and `uv sync` make the
project environment match `uv.lock` and `.python-version`, so pointed at
the `.venv` that `install.sh` built they remove PETSc, SLEPc and mpi4py or
replace the whole environment. uv resolves a relative `UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT`
against the repository root, so the commands below, run from the repository
root, keep the site environment in `docs/.venv-wiki`. Preview locally with
`UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT=docs/.venv-wiki uv run --only-group wiki mkdocs serve -f docs/mkdocs.yml`.
The gate is
`UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT=docs/.venv-wiki uv run --only-group wiki mkdocs build --strict -f docs/mkdocs.yml`
with zero warnings.

The site is published at `https://linstabpy.vercel.app/`, which the paper
cites. The maintainer deploys it from `docs/` with the Vercel CLI
(`vercel build`, then `vercel deploy --prebuilt`); `docs/vercel.json` holds the
build commands and the response headers. A push does not deploy.
`.github/workflows/docs.yml` runs the strict build on every pull request
that touches the pages, and publishes nothing.

## CHANGELOG discipline

- [Keep a Changelog](https://keepachangelog.com/) format.
- Every user-visible change gets an entry under `[Unreleased]` **as it lands**.
- Sections, in order: **Added / Changed / Fixed / Removed / Verified**.
- A withdrawn version number is never reused.

## Notes

- Plans and the task graph live in the private working repository, not here.
- Example PNGs under `examples/**/*.png` are tracked.
- Coverage on GitHub is the omit list (`src/` minus `solvers/`, `linalg/`,
  and the PETSc helpers). Do not set `fail_under` on the whole package.
